before: The only published protection note for this Grade III, 5.9, 7-pitch route is 'wide range of nuts and cams' - no exact sizes/counts are published. The route climbs cracks on the NW side of the buttress, starting on a steep slab with a thin vertical crack, with the crux on pitch 3.

No trip report or published description could be found describing this specific route's gear. Based on the stated 'Class 4 / low 5th' grade, a minimal rack is what the terrain implies: a few small-to-mid cams (roughly 0.3-1in) and 2-3 nuts to protect the brief low-5th move(s), plus a small handful of slings for a belay/rappel anchor. There is no basis for anything larger or for doubled gear — this is an inference from grade/terrain, not a verified rack list.

before: Hard slab crux described as a 'step up move w bolts at your face' — technical, balancy climbing rather than pulling on holds.
Off-trail approach is only informally marked.

This is the usual ascent line from the mountain's north side: traverse below the summit pyramid to reach the northeast ridge, crossing some steep gullies that hold snow, then follow the ridge crest to the summit with mostly class 3 and some class 4 moves. Total documented length is about 250 ft (76 m). The West Ridge is 'a more difficult and exposed' alternative by comparison.

Confirmed non-technical: 'the mountain does not require rope or rock climbing gear to summit' — Class 3 scramble up the west spur with one 4th-class move gaining the SW face; exposure but no fixed pro used.

Late June through early September, but conditions vary greatly by snow year — a late-June/early-July ascent found stable fresh snow, while another mid-July attempt in a low-snow year found the glacier 'more like early October,' with dangerous runout; check current NWAC/NPS conditions before committing.

Directly from the 2005 gear notes: a full set of wires, knifeblades, lost arrows, and Friends/cams from #1 to #3.5, plus 'a picket might have been nice.' Add a few short and medium ice screws — stubbies specifically, since the useful placements were in thin ice under an overhang and in the ice above the chockstone — a single rope, two technical ice tools and crampons. The pitons are not optional: the rock is compact and the party wrote that they were later 'very glad of the knifeblades' on the runout bulge below the chockstone. Belays were improvised from a cam, a stubby screw and a doubtful horn. Bring slings and tat for rappel anchors you may have to leave behind.

before.name: Harlequin Bridge / Campground shuttle stop
before.note: NPS shuttle stop where Stehekin Valley Road crosses the Stehekin River; start of the Stehekin River Trail approach toward Weaver Point.
before.directions: There is no road into Stehekin. Drive to Fields Point Landing or Chelan and take the Lady of the Lake II or Lady Express up-lake — two to four hours depending on which boat — then ride the National Park Service shuttle up the Stehekin Valley Road to the Harlequin Bridge stop. Some parties bike or walk the road instead. Sailings drop to a few a week outside peak summer, so build the trip around the boat schedule rather than the other way round.

before.name: Stehekin River Trail / Devore Creek Trail junction
before.note: Leave the flat Stehekin River Trail here and turn onto Devore Creek Trail #1244, which climbs steeply through rock bluffs into the Glacier Peak Wilderness.
before.directions: Cross Harlequin Bridge at the end of the airstrip and pick up the Stehekin River Trail on the far bank, heading downvalley. It is three essentially flat miles along the river to the junction, which sits about half a mile short of Weaver Point — parties who come in by water taxi to Weaver Point instead join this point from the other direction.

before.name: Bird Creek Camp
before.note: Small established bivy/camp used as base for Devore and Tupshin climbs; reliable water from Bird Creek nearby, last easy flat tent sites before the open basin.
before.directions: Turn uphill and climb hard: roughly 30 switchbacks in about two miles carry the trail through rock bluffs and open forest to the Wilderness boundary near 2,300 ft, and the grade stays relentless for another three-plus miles alongside Devore Creek. The tread through here sees little maintenance and is brushy underfoot. The creek is crossed and paralleled repeatedly and is the water source for the whole stretch.

before.name: Upper Bird Creek basin (~7,000 ft)
before.note: Open basin with small lakes below Devore; cross Bird Creek near the northern lake and head southeast toward the bench/gully leading to Devore's ridge.
before.directions: Leave the maintained trail and follow use paths and animal trails up along Bird Creek, gaining about a mile to an unofficial bench camp near 5,400 ft — parties wanting one big summit day often push to there instead. Gaining a hundred feet or so of hillside before sidehilling keeps the brush manageable; fighting up the creekbed does not. Above the bench the ground steepens into heather benches and a talus staircase, then a second looser gully of scree and dirt, before opening into the lake basin.

before.name: Saddle west of Point 7657
before.note: Col on Devore's southeast ridge reached via a snowfield/talus scramble from the basin; from here the route works west and traverses onto the peak's southeast face.
before.directions: Cross Bird Creek near the northern lake and climb loose Class 2-3 talus and scree southeast out of the basin to the col. Snow lingers here well into July and can leave a short traverse of around 40 degrees, so carry an axe and take crampons if it is likely to be firm. Loose rock and old avalanche debris are the other hazards on this stretch.

before.name: Exposed traverse below summit block
before.note: Class 3-4 ledge traverse across the southeast face to the summit ridge; reported as "extremely exposed 3rd class (4th?)" by climbers and the crux of the descent (reverse or short rappel).
before.directions: From the col, scramble west along the ridge crest, passing the pair of rock towers known locally as the Bottles. The crest then pushes you out onto the southeast face where it steepens and the ledge line begins. Rock quality is mixed — some of it solid, some of it slab under a layer of gravel.

before.name: Devore Peak summit
before.note: True summit at 8,383 ft on the long north-south ridge dividing Company/Hilgard Creek from Devore Creek; summit block requires a short downclimb or rappel on descent.
before.directions: Once across the traverse, scramble easier Class 2-3 ground up an obvious gully to the edge of the summit ridge. The last obstacle is a short, unavoidable rock face of about 20 ft, vertical and exposed. It is the one move on the route that most parties choose to rappel on the way down rather than downclimb.

before: Seven pitches of granite climbing up the South Face finishing with scrambling to the summit. P3 has loose rock leading to an airy belay below a 'cruxy roof and leaning crack.' P4-P5 offer 'solid, steep climbing on great granite,' with P5 holding the technical crux, a steep stemming chimney. P6 is described as 'a nice flourish to the route' with a hand-crack leading to an arete and another hand-crack. P7 is a short pitch that ends the technical climbing before scrambling to the summit.

Both counts are the same descent with a different rope setup. One published South Ridge description: "The rappel can be done in four raps with a 60M rope." The three stations listed here are the two-rope sequence — a short single-strand rappel from the summit bolts to the two-bolt station atop pitch 3, a double-rope rappel to the big ledge near the top of pitch 2, then one more to the base. Do not rappel straight from the summit to the top of pitch 2 on any setup: one rope falls about 15 ft short, and on two the crack below the anchor jams ropes.
Zebra Corner can seep water in early season, affecting climbing on that pitch.
The descent is notoriously easy to get wrong - 'has the potential of ruining your day.'
Expect some lichen and looseness typical of the wall's younger routes.
The approach gully has been described by parties as "involved and somewhat dangerous" — stay on route-finding beta rather than freelancing up the gully.
Early-season attempts can be very wet; water seeps affect the lower pitches into early summer.
The south-facing wall gets brutally hot in full summer sun — an alpine start is recommended.
Pitches 2-5 are strenuous with tough onsight sequences and limited rest stances.

Realistically a single enormous day: leave the car by first light, expect the better part of the day for the 2,600 ft of ledge navigation, and be on the summit early enough to start rappelling Infinite Bliss with hours of daylight in hand. Some parties bivy — the mountain's ascents 'generally require bivouacs or the longest days of summer'.
Mazamas describes this as 'car to car in two or more days' given the extra distance of crossing both glaciers.

From the North Fork Sauk River Trailhead (off Sloan Creek Road, FR 49), follow North Fork Sauk Trail #649 up the valley through old-growth forest, past the Red Creek bridge to Mackinaw Shelter, then up a long series of switchbacks to meet the Pacific Crest Trail at about 5,950 ft, roughly 8-9 miles from the car. White Pass and its camp are a short way south along the PCT; this route does not go there. Turn north on the PCT and cross Red Pass (about 6,500 ft) a mile or two on, then descend into the upper White Chuck valley and follow the PCT down it for roughly 7-9 miles, past the old White Chuck River Trail junction (~3,850 ft), to a forested campsite near 4,100 ft beside Sitkum Creek. There, leave the maintained trail on the unsigned, unmaintained climbers' path (locally described as 'more like a fisherman's route than a trail'), which goes straight up the forested ridge south of Sitkum Creek to Boulder Basin (5,500-6,000 ft), where the trees break and the standard high camp sits on heather and rock benches with running water nearby. From camp, ascend snowfields southeast onto the toe of the Sitkum Glacier. The old approach up the White Chuck River Trail past Kennedy Hot Springs to the same PCT junction is no longer usable: the White Chuck Road (FR 23) is closed to vehicles at milepost 3.7, and the trail has been listed as inaccessible since the October 2003 flood. Going out, the PCT climbs back up the valley and over Red Pass before the long descent to the car.

A four-station sequence of 50/50/50/20 m is sometimes attached to this route. It matches, figure for figure, a published trip report for north Gunsight Peak's West Face — a 5.11+, 6-pitch, 600 ft rock route on a different summit — and does not belong to this Class 5.6 glacier route on the main spire. Nothing about those figures was measured here, so they are not carried. What is documented for this route is two double-rope rappels: "We belayed each other back down the exposed summit ridge, then made a double-rope rappel down the west face", and then "a diagonal double-rope rappel, putting in directional protection along the way, which allowed us to reach the snow finger in one shot." That party carried two 60 m ropes. No single-rope descent of this route is documented.

Most parties reverse the West Ridge: from the true (west) summit, downclimb the class 3-4 ridge crest back toward the notch/saddle used on the way up, staying on the north side of the crest per the standard line and reversing the short crux step (a ~6 ft downclimb at a minor notch). Many parties downclimb this cleanly, but a single short rappel (roughly 15 m/50 ft, well within a 30 m single-rope length) is commonly used here instead, especially in wet conditions or with less experienced climbers — anchors are natural (slung horns/blocks or a small nut/cam placement backed by a cordelette), not bolted; there's no fixed hardware on this route. From the saddle, either reverse the ascent couloir into Lundin Basin (a fast glissade of up to 1,200-1,500 ft when it's still snow-filled, typically only reliable early season) or walk scree/talus down toward the Red-Lundin col to pick up the use trail back into Commonwealth Basin and the PCT. An alternative some parties use is descending the East Ridge instead: scramble down the crest about 100 ft to the top of a small cliff band, then make one single-rope rappel (30 m is sufficient; natural tree/horn anchors — the ridge has 'lots of trees to sling') down to easy ledges, continuing to a notch in the ridge crest from which an early-season glissade or scramble rejoins the standard route in Lundin/Commonwealth Basin. This option requires either looping back on foot into Commonwealth Basin or a car shuttle/hitch between the Alpental and PCT-North trailheads, since the two approaches start at different lots. Bottom line for planning: expect zero to one short rappel (under 15 m, single rope, natural gear anchors — no bolts) — conditions and party comfort level determine whether it's downclimbed or rapped. Total descent to the trailhead runs roughly 2-2.5 hours in trip reports.

Descend by reversing the final scramble pitches/downclimbing back to the top of the technical face (the uppermost section is a downclimb/scramble to the top of the East Face), then begin a rappel sequence rather than trying to downclimb the buttress itself — the rock is loose enough that down-climbing the route is not recommended. From a small ledge/anchor on the east side just below the summit, a 50 m rappel gets you down the steepest upper wall (rockfall-prone — the next rappeller should move off to the side immediately, not straight down, to avoid anyone above). Below that, parties generally find 2-3 more rappel stations working down toward the notch system: a single 60 m rappel to a belay/anchor stance, followed by an overhanging section that's typically rappelled on doubled rope (i.e., a full 60 m rope folded, giving ~28-30 m of rappel) down to just below (north side of) Gunsight Notch/the V-notch. Accounts are not fully consistent on the exact count — some describe essentially 3 key rappels down this line, others log 4, and one description notes '5 rappels will get you down... a 60 m rope is long enough' — the variance reflects rope length used and which anchors parties link together. Plan on 4-5 rappels with a single 60 m rope (or 2x 30 m/60 m doubled) to be safe, and treat 3 as an optimistic minimum if you're able to link stations with a full 60 m strand. Anchors are natural/fixed, not bolted: expect slung trees, horns, and boulders with aging webbing/cord — inspect every anchor before weighting it, back it up if it looks tired, and carry a knife and spare cord/webbing since parties have had to replace or rebuild anchors mid-descent. The first station below the staircase is reportedly in a tree at the top of the drop overlooking the V-notch. Once down to the notch, reverse the snow/scree gully and the traverse back across Mixup's east flank to Cascade Pass and out the trail to the trailhead; if you camped at Cache Col/Kool-Aid Lake, break camp there instead of continuing all the way to the car. Watch for rockfall from parties above throughout the descent, and be alert for a moated-out Cache Col in late season if that's part of your exit.

Monte Cristo Peak (7,136 ft) is the technical centerpiece of the Monte Cristo Group, a tight cluster of peaks (Kyes, Cadet, Columbia, Del Campo) ringing the ghost town of Monte Cristo in the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness. Unlike its neighbors, Monte Cristo has no scramble-only line to the true summit: the standard and most-climbed route, the North Col Route, requires roped 5.6 rock climbing through a short chimney above the col, so it's properly a Basic Alpine Climb rather than a Class 3 scramble. The peak was first climbed in 1923 by James M. Keyes and W. Zerum, and in 1918 was called 'a huge pile of red rock.'

A standard rack to 2 inches (cams and nuts) covers the route; published descriptions specifically call for a 'rock rack to 2 in.' A single rack with extra slings is sufficient for parties simul-climbing the sustained low-5th-class sections, saving weight on the long approach.

Often described as the 'Southeast Slope-Southeast Ridge' or simply the south-slope route, this is the standard and effectively only reasonable way up Mount Carru. From the Carru-Lago col/saddle area, a scree-and-talus gully drops toward the south; parties ascend this gully (weaving around a few short rock steps/cliff bands), and once the terrain opens up and flattens near the col, turn and follow the broad southeast ridge/upper south slopes to the summit. The peak's north side is a steep, cliffed face and is not part of any standard route. As a climb it is unremarkable technically -- 'just a scree and talus heap with many parallel ribs' -- and is usually combined with neighboring Mount Lago and/or Osceola Peak in the same trip since all three summits sit within a mile or two of one another.

Descend the same trail. In early season (roughly April–June) the snow-filled chute below the summit basin is commonly glissaded, but it is a southeast-facing, sun-exposed avalanche funnel that can turn to wet-slide hazard by early-mid afternoon — go early, check NWAC, and carry/know how to self-arrest with an ice axe. The Forest Service specifically warns the chute's bordering rocks are 'extremely slick when wet or foggy.'

weather.probability: A single storm system mid-route can strand or endanger a party on exposed towers; afternoon instability is a recurring concern through the summer

Recorded only briefly as a 'difficult Bryan Burdo alpine rock climb' on Persis's north face — no detailed grade, pitch count, or topo is available. This is a serious, low-traffic line distinct from the peak's Class 2 West Ridge hiking route; treat it as an alpine rock objective requiring full trad rack, rope, and North Cascades route-finding/approach skills rather than a hiking route.

before: The standard, non-technical route up Mount Stuart and the standard descent for every technical ridge/face route on the mountain. From the false summit (~9,200 ft) it's a short, exposed Class 2-3 scramble east along the ridge to the true summit. Fred Beckey called Stuart "without a rival as the crown peak in the central Cascades of Washington", and this route is the one most often photographed from Longs Pass.

Start at the Tubal Cain Trailhead (elev. ~3,300 ft, reached via FR 2870/2880), and follow the Tubal Cain Trail #840 (Copper Creek drainage) south. The trail climbs gently through second-growth and old-growth conifer forest, gaining roughly 1,900 ft over the first ~5.5-6 miles. At about 3 miles, pass the signed junction with the Tull Canyon Trail #847 (a steep 0.6-mile side spur to a 1952 B-17 crash site) and continue straight on #840. Around 0.5 mile past that junction the trail crosses Copper Creek near the historic Tubal Cain Mine tailings (last reliable, easy water before the lake), then switchbacks up through subalpine meadows toward Buckhorn Pass. Watch for the unsigned or lightly-signed spur (near ~5,200 ft, roughly 5.5-6 miles in) that drops left/southwest to Buckhorn Lake -- it's easy to miss ('don't miss the left turn to Buckhorn Lake'). Follow this spur down to the lake, which is the last dependable water source before the summit push. From the south end of Buckhorn Lake the maintained tread disappears; cross the inlet stream/waterfall at the head of the lake and pick up a faint boot path heading southwest into avalanche-damaged timber (expect blowdown and light bushwhacking). This opens into a broad, flat bench of avalanche debris about 200 ft above the lake -- the true start of the off-trail scramble. From there climb a wide talus/scree gully trending south then curving east, breaking treeline around 5,800 ft (roughly 700 ft above the lake), where the going turns to loose rock and light class 2-3 scrambling. Angle east/southeast up increasingly loose slopes to gain the Iron-Worthington col at approximately 6,420 ft. Hazards on this leg: avalanche debris and blowdown near the lake, sustained loose scree/talus underfoot above treeline (helmet recommended for rockfall from parties above), and route-finding through the faint, unmarked path -- a GPS track or detailed written beta is strongly advised since cairns are sparse. From the Iron-Worthington col, angle northeast up open slopes to the base of Worthington's summit fin; the final class 3 scramble drops a few feet left of the ridge crest to a short (~10 ft) crack, then follows the top of the fin to the true summit.

The climbing is described as "hard and sustained" 5.9. A 2004 forum thread discusses whether chockstones in the chimney offer protection every 20-30 ft through the crux; no definitive answer was given, so treat it as a serious, sparsely-protected lead. Pitch count and length are not recorded.

Two long approaches reach Whatcom Pass (~5,200 ft), and both are roughly comparable in mileage (~16-17 miles one-way). From the west: start at the Hannegan Pass Trailhead (end of Hannegan Pass Rd/FS-32, ~3,100 ft) and follow Trail #674 about 4 miles/2,000 ft to Hannegan Pass (~5,050-5,100 ft), then descend the far side to Boundary Camp in the Chilliwack River valley. Continue down-valley on the Chilliwack River Trail (unmaintained and rough in sections, with stretches obliterated by avalanche debris) past Copper Creek Camp, then turn up the Brush Creek Trail junction and climb through US Cabin Camp, Graybeal Camp, and Whatcom Camp to Whatcom Pass — a long day or more typically split over 2 days with a valley-bottom camp. A cable-car crossing of the Chilliwack River exists near U.S. Cabin Camp as an alternative to fording. From the east: hire a water taxi from Ross Lake Resort (near Diablo, off SR 20) to the Little Beaver Creek trailhead (~1,600 ft) on Ross Lake, then follow the Little Beaver Trail roughly 16 miles up-valley — passing Perry Creek Camp at 4.6 miles and Twin Rocks Camp around mile 8, then the Big Beaver Trail junction at 10.5 miles — before the final steep switchback climb through big-fir forest up to Whatcom Pass. Whichever way you arrive, from Whatcom Pass a faint, informal climbers' trail leaves the maintained trail and heads directly south, gaining the broad toe of Whatcom Peak's north ridge; the path quickly gives way to snow patches and broken rock, and route-finding is 'stay on the crest' rather than following any marked line.

before: The stored count of 2 was a partial count of the same sequence. A detailed descent report gives all three: "Two single-rope rappels got us down to the wide ledge", then from the saddle "we set up a double-rope rappel from the highest anchor... one double-rope rappel was just enough to reach the glacier below." no published account gives how a single-rope party gets off the saddle, so plan on two ropes.

From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (FS Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road), follow the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599) — 4 miles, 2,280 ft gain, crossing Mountaineer Creek on a log bridge at 1.5 miles, staying right at the Lake Stuart Trail junction, finishing with a boulder-moraine climb to the outlet (2.5-3 hours). Top off water here. Head toward the lake's south/east side onto the cairned Aasgard Pass climbers' trail, gaining talus/heather to about 400 ft above the lake (30-40 min, watch for wet snow into July), then cut climber's-left through dense slide-alder/heather brush (15-20 minutes) to the base gully system. Scarface climbs the gully just left of the West Face route's start; route beta specifically flags this terrain as 'very loose and exposed,' so extra care with rope-up/spacing is warranted through the final approach scramble. Total trailhead-to-base time runs about 3.5-4 hours, in line with neighboring routes.

Approach via Downey Creek Trail to high camp at Cub Lake or Itswoot Ridge (5,400-6,400 ft). Traverse Chickamin Glacier to Dome-Sinister col at approximately 8,450 feet. Contour around Sinister's south side via easy snowfield, then climb a prominent loose gully (Class 3, loose rock) to the ridge. Ascend the upper west ridge via Class 2-3 snow and scrambling to the roomy summit. Total time from camp approximately 3-4 hours. The southwest gully is notably loose—one well-documented party described it as 'one of the loosest, most unpleasant gullies we've ever had the displeasure of climbing.' Descent can reverse via the gully or traverse to the lower west ridge (white-knuckle Class 3-4 scrambling with fixed sling protection at one crux).

weather.typical: Same maritime North Cascades pattern as the rest of the range: drier July-August windows with fast-changing fog/wind/rain still possible
weather.probability: Thunderstorm risk is low relative to the Cascades' east side; changeable, low-visibility weather is the more likely hazard, which matters more on this longer, more sustained ridge

before.exposure: Longer and more sustained exposure than the West Ridge ('steady Class 3 and 4 scrambling'); exposure on the crest specifically, and the extra length increases cumulative fall consequence

avalanche.zone: N/A - summer alpine rock route with a short glacier crossing; nearest NWAC coverage is the general Mt Baker area with no dedicated Twin Sisters Range forecast, and the route is normally climbed only after avalanche season ends

before.crevasses: The standard approach crosses a moat at the North Twin-South Twin saddle to gain the Sisters Glacier, then travels the glacier (a bergschrund can form partway across, worse late season) before climbing to the North Ridge crest - rope up for this crossing.

before: From the Depot Creek trailhead parking on the abandoned logging spur off Chilliwack Lake Road (BC) at roughly 2,350 ft, hike the old roadway grade uphill (left-hand fork) for about a mile to the Monument 65 border marker, where you cross into North Cascades National Park and should sign in at the wilderness-permit kiosk. From there the route follows the unmaintained, unmarked 'Depot Creek climbers path' — a boot-track through old-growth forest for roughly 3 miles that gains to the base of Depot Creek Falls (about 4.8 hours and 1,600 ft in from the cars per one detailed trip log). The falls are one of the tallest in Washington (drop cited around 900-1,000 ft), and the path climbs steep, often wet and slippery slabs along its left edge; a fixed handline is present at the crux scramble section here and this is the approach's main technical hazard (exposed, greasy rock, worse in the wet or in the dark — several parties report losing the tread here at night). Above the falls the path eases through scrubby subalpine forest onto a broad outwash plain, reaching treeline where climbers typically switch to mountaineering boots/crampons. Continue up class 3 tread gaining roughly 800 ft into the Redoubt Glacier basin; Ouzel Lake, in this basin, is the most common first camp. From Ouzel Lake most parties relocate camp 3-4 hours further up onto the Redoubt Glacier saddle/col (~7,150 ft) for a high camp closer to the peaks — this leg is flat glacier travel with only minor, usually avoidable crevasse hazard in normal late-season conditions. From high camp, traverse roughly 2 miles east across snow/glacier beneath Easy Mox's south side toward the 'Col of the Wild,' the saddle between Easy and Hard (Southeast) Mox, finishing with a steep ~1,000 ft climb over notoriously unstable, sandy talus (loose rock is the dominant hazard on this whole upper approach — helmets on well before the col). From the Col of the Wild, ascend a ramp leading right past a snow patch into a gully, then scramble up and right (class 4, exposed enough that many parties belay it) toward a notch in the 'Ridge of Gendarmes.' A short sequence of ledges zig-zagging right-left-right leads through the notch; descend briefly to a small flat area and locate the correct gully leading to a high notch on the west ridge, which is the start of the roped climbing (two pitches of 5th class to the summit tower, then a final short, exposed class 3 scramble — stay roped — to the true summit). Water is available from the glacier/snowmelt and Ouzel Lake but not reliably along the upper ridge, so carry enough from camp.

sectionBreakdown.note: "One of the harder, more sustained lines on SEWS's south face (5.11d free, or 5.9+ C1) — 9 pitches make for a long, technical day with the same approach and South Arete downclimb/rappel descent as its neighbors."

before: Spectre Peak (7,952'; listsofjohn.com's LIDAR-based figure is 7,953') sits on the western slope of the Northern Pickets — it's grouped thematically with neighboring Ghost Peak and Phantom Peak near Swiss Peak and Mount Challenger, part of the Northern Pickets traverse line (Luna-Fury-Swiss-Spectre-Phantom-Crooked Thumb-Ghost-Challenger). It is one of the most remote and rarely climbed summits in the Pickets, with only two documented technical routes on record: Haunted Wall (IV 5.9+, 2,100', Wayne Wallace and Mike Layton, Aug 2006) and this South Ridge line.

A more technical, low-5th-class ridge scramble/climb on Sperry's south side - harder and more interesting than the standard route but without the commitment of the north/east face lines. It is heavily vegetated and "not a recommended route" for quality, though it is a real, documented line.
Mostly bolted; described as 'bolts with smallish trad gear' on the crux pitch and 'mixed gear and bolts above' — bring a light trad rack in addition to draws.

Fred Beckey reportedly attempted this face earlier and found it traumatic enough to never return, and historians called it a "Last Great Problem" that "should probably remain" unclimbed. Layton and Wolfe finally forced a route in 2005 after a brutal approach, climbing banded gneiss that offered very little solid protection; every hold reportedly required testing, and pitons often wouldn't set. Note: the grade/length is variously given as V+ 5.9+ A2- and ~2,500 ft, and as V+ 5.11- and 2,400 ft — the latter figures are used here, but treat the discrepancy as a sign of how approximate any grade is on this kind of loose, unrepeated wall.

Best climbed in dry, settled conditions from mid-summer into September; the approach gully becomes hazardous (loose, wet rock) in bad weather, so this is explicitly "not a climb to do with iffy weather." Snow can linger in the gully earlier in the season; water is available near the base in early September.

After camping at Spectacle Point (5,800 ft), the route climbs the West Ridge and West Face of West Peak to the summit — described simply as 'rock scramble and rock climb,' i.e. class 3-4 terrain without a documented technical crux comparable to the Middle Peak chimney.
From Smithbrook Rd/Union Gap, bushwhack NE to gain the SE ridge and follow it to the summit. Described explicitly as an 'easy to moderate, non-technical alpine scramble.'

Painted Mountain (historically called Red Mountain, and known to local Native peoples by the Lushootseed name 'Ska-hala-bats,' meaning 'painted') is a striking, mineral-streaked 6,975 ft summit of Late Cretaceous migmatitic gneiss in the western Glacier Peak Wilderness southeast of Darrington. Its reddish-orange rock gives the peak its name and its distinctive 'huge massif of red rocks' summit block. A now-abandoned fire lookout once stood near the top, part of the dense early-1900s North Cascades lookout network; the peak was likely first climbed around 1897 by a USGS survey party. It's reached via a short maintained trail followed by a well-known, unmaintained climber's path up the southwest ridge.

From the summit, rappel the west side of the two main gendarmes, then scramble down and around the west slope on good-to-loose boulders and scree, avoiding the north summit route, and return to high camp.

The published rack note is simply a 'wide range of nuts and cams', which for a 1970s crack line of this character means a genuinely full standard rack rather than a specialised one. A practical kit: a full set of wired nuts (small brass through large), a single set of cams from about BD #0.3 to #3 with doubles in the #0.5 to #2 hand sizes that make up most of the climbing, and one #4 if you want security in the wider dihedral sections. Bring a dozen alpine draws — the cracks wander and the pitches are long, so extend generously to keep rope drag out of a seven-pitch day. Nuts and small cams also serve for gear anchors; there is no fixed gear on the route. A single 60 m rope is sufficient since there is no rappel descent.

July.reason: Early-month snow can still linger on the approach and lower ridge; conditions firm up to the best-season window by mid-month

August.reason: Peak dry-granite conditions ('best with dry granite and a melted-out approach')

September.reason: Stable, cool weather, but shorter days add pressure to a route already timed at ~10 hours round trip from bivy

before: Do not plan to reverse the technical wall — virtually every account of climbing Baring's north face describes descending a separate walk-off line rather than rappelling the route from top to bottom. From the top of the wall, traverse west/climber's-left (some parties describe following an old 'base-jumper' boot path) around to a talus field and the notch between Baring's summits, then drop roughly 700 vertical feet through boulders and meadow to pick up a heather trail on skier's left. This connects to a game trail switchbacking down through old-growth forest, a roughly one-mile traverse along the ridgecrest, and then a steep switchbacking trail (~1,500 vertical ft) down to a clearing and old logging road that returns to the Barclay Lake Trailhead — about 3 hours car-to-summit-to-car for the descent leg on the routes this has been documented for. This walk-off is a scramble/hike, not a rappel descent, and no fixed rappel stations are established on it. That said, treat this as route- and finish-dependent: Baring's north face has multiple independent lines topping out at different points, some of which may not connect cleanly to the walk-off gully without downclimbing or short rope work, and the original 1961 first-ascent account explicitly describes 'long rappels down the upper walls' to retreat/descend in fog when the walk-off wasn't known or reachable. If you retreat mid-route, or finish on a line that doesn't top out near the notch, be prepared to rappel — carry a 60m rope and rack for building anchors, since fixed/bolted rappel stations should not be assumed on this poorly-protected, historically loose-rock alpine wall; natural anchors (trees, horns, gear) are the norm. Given this uncertainty, treat rappel count as route-specific and unknown rather than fixed.

From the Phelps Creek Trailhead (~3,500 ft, end of FR 6211), start on the wide, gently graded Phelps Creek Trail #1511 heading north/upstream along Phelps Creek through open forest. In roughly 0.25–0.4 mile, watch for a signed junction and bear right (steeply uphill) onto the narrower Carne Mountain Trail — this is the last easy water for a while, so top off here or at the small creeklet just past the junction, since the climb above is essentially dry except for early-season snowmelt. From the junction the trail 'gets right down to business,' switchbacking up through open forest, vine maple, and beargrass slopes and gaining about 2,600 ft in the next 2.9 miles — a sustained, steep grade with little flat respite. Around 3.1–3.2 miles from the trailhead you top out at a broad saddle near 6,800 ft with a sweeping view of Mount Maude, Seven Fingered Jack, Clark Mountain, and Glacier Peak; this saddle is also the junction with the climbers'/unmaintained Rock Creek Trail heading east. From the saddle, bear left and switchback up open talus and scree for a final 0.4–0.5 mile to the summit at 7,091 ft, passing near a minor false high point along the way. The standard route is Class 1–2 the entire way (a steep trail/talus walk, no technical scrambling), but snow can linger on the upper switchbacks and around the saddle into early-mid July, and the exposed saddle/ridge can be windy — an ice axe is worth carrying for early-season snow patches near the top. There is no ford of Phelps Creek on this route (the trail junction is well before any major crossing); the only route-finding subtlety is picking the correct fork at the Phelps Creek/Carne Mountain junction low down and staying on-trail through the talus near the summit block.

before.optimalWindow: Mid-July through early September ("mid-summer through early fall while the glacier is well-covered")

July.reason: Start of the optimal window; glacier travel conditions improve through the month but bridges are still transitioning early on.

June.reason: Full snow cover and avalanche-prone conditions persist into spring; glacier crevasses are still snow-bridged, which hides rather than eliminates crevasse-fall risk, and steep-snow skills are essential.

August.reason: Core of the recommended season - glacier typically best-covered and most stable, though crevasses begin opening later in the month.

October.reason: Snow returns in fall; conditions shift toward full winter alpine and SR 20 access can become unreliable ahead of its seasonal closure.

September.reason: Early fall is 'stable early, then snow returns' - still within the recommended window but crevasses are most open and the weather window is narrowing.

before: The two stored numbers count different things and neither was wrong. The 2 half-rope rappels are encountered ON the ridge extension as part of the route, from fixed tat reported as dated — back it up. The summit descent is separate: the West Ridge is described as bolted chain anchors where "a 60m rope was just long enough for some of those rappels", or "more than a dozen rappels back down the South Buttress" if you reverse the line instead.
condition-dependent glacier crevasses/moats — one low-snow mid-July attempt found the glacier 'more like early October,' with dangerous runout requiring belayed climbing
loose Class 4-5 ledges around the north-ridge pinnacles
sandy, insecure ledges below the summit headwall
cold bivouac risk if the summit day runs late

Poor to marginal throughout. The lower band is compact gneiss and was simul-climbed with long gaps between pieces; the crux traverse across a partially iced slab was described as terrain where 'falling would not be good, so he thoughtfully doesn't'. Pins are the primary protection. The one properly protected move on the route is the chockstone itself — a cam below the roof and a stubby screw in the good ice on the left. On the upper couloir and rib, expect simul-climbing with occasional gear and very large exposure. Nothing about this route rewards a cam-only rack.

before.peakTraffic: Rarely climbed even in peak summer months; described by multiple trip-report sources as 'almost unknown by climbers, let alone tourists'
before.estimatePerSeason: Likely fewer than 10-15 parties per season; no formal visitor counts exist for this objective

before: Rock across the whole formation is loose, fragmented shale/sandstone/pillow-basalt — NPS explicitly calls Olympic rock "loose, fragmented and chossy" and dangerous.
No fixed protection or rappel anchors are documented anywhere on Steeple Rock.
Very little is known about this route, which sees few repeats
A second new route, 'Lily of the West,' was established on the same day/trip on Dome Peak's South Face area, but no separate pitch or grade beta for it could be verified

Widely described as 'nothing more than a walk' once the Lucky Pass col is reached — the difficulty of this route lies almost entirely in the approach (creek crossing, steep brushy ridge gain, and a glacier traverse), not the summit scramble itself. Most parties treat it as a 2-3 day backcountry trip out of Colonial Creek Campground.

Same trailhead and lower approach as the East Ridge: Eldorado Trailhead at Cascade River Road mile 20 (~2,100 ft), cross the Cascade River via the log/three-tree crossing about 90 ft downstream of the parking area, then climb the steep timbered climbers' trail into a dry boulderfield (roughly to 4,500 ft) and on into Eldorado Creek Basin. From there, rather than continuing over the ridge into Roush Basin toward the standard East Ridge camp, this route stays on/traverses over the Roush Divide and ascends the Eldorado Glacier, trending toward the Eldorado–Dean's Spire col on the mountain's northwest side to reach the wild Marble Creek Cirque, with views of Dorado Needle and Early Morning Spire. The approach to this face is longer and more involved than the East Ridge approach — described in route notes as "guarded by a long, somewhat complicated approach" across glaciated and crevassed terrain, so rope up for the glacier sections. High camp is typically established either in Eldorado Creek/Roush Creek Basin or higher at the Eldorado-Inspiration Glacier site (~7,500–7,600 ft). One recorded ascent (climbing from the trailhead in a single push) took roughly 5 hours to reach the couloir's base; that party also used a shortcut of a belayed downclimb (~35 m) and two 30-meter rappels down a snow/rock gully near the Eldorado–Dean's Spire col to drop directly to within about 100 yards of the couloir, which meaningfully shortens the standard glacier traverse but is a variation, not the only way in — most parties simply continue glacier travel around to the couloir's base at about 7,800 ft. Hazards on approach: crevasses on the Eldorado/Inspiration Glaciers, a long featureless glacier crossing that can be disorienting in whiteout, and the optional gully downclimb/rappel shortcut is itself exposed snow-and-rock terrain.

This is the generic 'easiest route' taken by nearly every party that visits Emerald Peak, almost always as a side-summit from a basin camp shared with Cardinal and/or Saska Peak. It is described consistently as: gain a basin around 6,800-6,900 ft below the Cardinal-Emerald saddle, cross talus/scree to the base of a broad gully, climb the gully (moderate snow early season, loose scree/rock later) to a notch in the summit ridge, then turn and scramble class 2-3 rock (described as short — 'a very short class 3 scramble near the top') to the summit. This line has no formal name; 'Southeast Ridge' describes the ridge/notch it gains relative to Cardinal Peak, which sits just SE of Emerald.

About five single-rope rappels, roughly 400 ft total, down the rock rib beside the snow couloir - one published account gives 'five or six single rope rappels from here back to the snowfield' for the same line. Three is reported in good early-season snow, when much of the couloir is downclimbed instead, and six to seven in dry late-season conditions when the snow has pulled back off the rock. All of these are single-rope figures; two ropes roughly halves them. Do not reverse the Northeast Face itself.

Ghost Peak is normally climbed as an add-on from a high camp shared with neighboring Crooked Thumb Peak and Phantom Peak, since all three summits are within a few tenths of a mile of one another in the Northern Pickets. Access from camp is 'obvious' once you're established there. The first-ascent party's own account: 'The route was from the notch south of the peak which was gained from the west. We stayed on the south and west sides of the mountain following obvious weaknesses' — easy-to-moderate 4th/low-5th-class climbing on comparatively solid Pickets rock.

before.name: Downey Creek Trailhead
before.note: Trail #768 into Glacier Peak Wilderness off Suiattle River Road; self-issue wilderness permit and Northwest Forest Pass/day-use fee at the kiosk.

before.name: Bachelor Creek crossing
before.note: Downey Creek Trail ends here on a sturdy log bridge over Bachelor Creek; the steep, unmaintained Bachelor Creek climbers' path continues uphill from the far bank.
before.directions: Follow Downey Creek Trail #768 up the valley on maintained tread that climbs only gently for most of its length. You cross five tributary creeks along the way, and the one draining Downey and Pilot Lakes can be a difficult ford in spring runoff. Expect old-growth blowdown across the tread in places and a brushy avalanche-chute crossing opposite Green Mountain; informal camps appear at roughly 1.6, 3, 3.5 and 4 miles if you need to break the day.

before.name: Bachelor Flats / Bachelor Meadows
before.note: Informal, well-used forest camp in a flat basin; standard Day 1 stop before the alpine terrain above.
before.directions: From the far bank the climbers' path follows the north side of Bachelor Creek. Parties report an improved use-trail through here that bypasses the older, brushier line lower down, and it is worth finding because this is the slowest ground of the day. It climbs steadily to the flat basin above.

before.name: Cub Pass (above Cub Lake)
before.note: Steep snow slopes lead to this pass overlooking often still-frozen Cub Lake; can hold near-full snow coverage into midsummer, so watch for glissade/postholing hazard.
before.directions: Continue up steepening open slopes above the meadows to the pass. There is no maintained tread from here on, and route-finding through this section and on up to Itswoot Ridge is one of the approach's real difficulties in cloud or flat light.

before.name: Itswoot Ridge camp
before.note: Flat meadow camp on the ridge with a stream fed from Spire Col; open views across to the Dome Glacier and Dome Peak, common Day 2 camp.
before.directions: Drop roughly 700 ft off the far side of the pass to Cub Lake, then cross the meadows beyond it and climb back up to gain Itswoot Ridge and Itswoot Pass. That descent is the one substantial loss of height on the approach, and it has to be re-climbed on the way out.

before.name: Dome Glacier crossing
before.note: Roped glacier travel below Dome Peak on the way to the Chikamin-Dome col; crevasses are usually narrow enough to step across in-season but require glacier travel skills.
before.directions: From Itswoot Pass the route steps straight off rock and snow onto the ice, so rope up at the edge rather than partway across. The line traverses east below Dome Peak toward the col rather than climbing the glacier directly.

before.name: Chikamin-Dome Col
before.note: Well-established high camp/col at the base of the technical climbing between Chikamin and Dome Peaks; watch for a bergschrund near the col.
before.directions: Keep traversing east across the glacier and climb the final slope to the col at about 8,500 ft. The bergschrund below it is the one obstacle worth scouting before you commit to a line. Reaching this point is over 7,000 ft of cumulative gain from the road.

before.name: Gunsight Peak summit
before.note: Tiny horn-shaped summit block ("the size of a barstool") reached via a Class 5.6 dihedral crux and short chimneys/cracks up to Class 5.5 along the exposed ridge crest.
before.directions: From the col the route drops before it climbs: a descending traverse of roughly 90 minutes reaches a snow bench and rock outcrop on the Chikamin Glacier around 7,000-7,500 ft directly under Gunsight's west face, and some parties move camp there rather than crossing the glacier twice. Above the bench, cross the bergschrund and take a short Class 3-4 wall to a broad ledge, then move left into the black basaltic dihedral whose uppermost 15 ft is the exposed 5.6 crux. Scramble the reddish-black dike above it, downclimb about 20 ft at the Main-North notch and traverse right across steep broken rock, then follow short chimneys and cracks to the ridge crest beside a large horn thickly slung with rappel webbing. The dike and upper gully hold loose rock and the gendarmed ridge is easy to misread in cloud, so fix that horn in mind — it confirms you are on line in both directions.

before: A standard alpine trad rack for 5.10 crack and face climbing; no specific inventory was published beyond 'the rope and rack.'
One climber described the route as 'very steep and fun,' taking about 3 hours from upper Royal Lake Basin to the top.
The couloir's reliable window is short and spring-specific — check recent trip reports for current conditions before planning around it.

First climbed in 1998 by Mark Bunker and Mike Press. Starts near the right side of the south face on steep, sandy, broken rock with shallow cracks, then a second pitch moving slightly left reaches the summit at mid-5th-class difficulty. Described by the first-ascent party as 'a fun day out.'

Documentation of this line is sparse, and there is no full route description. Climbers who have scouted it describe very poor rock overall — 'as bad as anything in the Olympics' near the summit ridge — with a possible band of somewhat better rock on the north side, but caution that any existing description should be taken 'with a grain of salt' and the line ground-truthed in person.

Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the summit gully back to the ~7,400 ft bench, then work back east along the south-slope traverse, staying on or near the outbound line (cairns mark the route in places) to bypass the Grotesque Gendarmes buttress (a short 4th-class downclimb with real exposure) before regaining the sidehill traverse back toward Easy Pass and the maintained trail. This is a walk-off/downclimb route with no fixed rappel stations reported — a winter ascent trip report on this same peak explicitly noted the party chose to downclimb rather than rappel because there were 'no obvious solid anchor points' on the upper mountain, consistent with the loose/fractured granite and slate character of the terrain. A rope, a few slings, and gear for natural anchors (horns, chockstones) are worth carrying as a contingency for a short rappel around the gendarmes or a wet/icy gully, but the standard descent for this route is downclimbing, not rappelling. Main hazards: loose rock and 4th-class exposure at the gendarme bypass, potential snow/runout in the gully early season, and the same tricky waterfall/scree crossing on the return traverse that made the approach route-finding nontrivial — down-climbing steep scree in this section in worsening light or weather is the most commonly cited crux of the whole outing.

before.peakTraffic: Described by Climbing.com as "one of the more popular routes on the wall" on Liberty Bell's East Face — it shares the same popular approach/wall as the much-climbed Thin Red Line, boosting its relative traffic versus other harder East Face lines.
before.estimatePerSeason: Dozens per season among 5.12 free climbers (low-medium confidence estimate)

before: Grade V alpine, 5.9 YDS, 26 pitches, approximately 2,000 ft (606 m) of climbing. Route composition: Beckey Route on Liberty Bell (5.3-5.6), North Face of Concord Tower, North Face of Lexington Tower, Northwest Corner of North Early Winter Spire (5.9+), Southwest Rib of South Early Winter Spire. Hazards include significant rockfall danger in approach gully ("bowling alley for rocks"), exposed alpine terrain, route finding challenges. Requires excellent trad climbing skills, solid alpine rock climbing experience, and good protection/anchor placement ability. Standard rack with couple bigger pieces for North Early Winter Spire. Short rappel descent from summits. The individual summits, the Beckey Route above all, are busy on summer weekends, though few parties do the full traverse. Best season: July-August during optimal weather windows. Typically done as 1-2 day alpine climb with experienced parties.
The rock quality is described as 'great' on the lower ridge but 'looser' higher up — take extra care with hand and foot placements above the crux section.
This same terrain is scrambled ropeless by strong parties in good conditions (see the app's 'Twin Sisters Olivine Scramble' entry).

The Northeast Couloir is the snow alternative to the North Face and shares its entire approach. From Pelton Basin, climb easy slopes and a steep couloir onto the Yawning Glacier (which spans roughly 6,200 to 6,800 ft), and follow the glacier to the Magic–Pelton Col at 6,480 ft. From there, instead of traversing west to the north face, take the couloir directly to the summit — the published description allows for either rock or snow depending on the year and the season. Skiers know the northeast line as the Banana Couloir and describe it as consistently steep but wide, winding about 2,000 ft down Magic Mountain's shoulder, with a lower half around 40-45 degrees, an upper section at 45-50, and a proper 50 degrees at the very top. Trip reports on this aspect consistently flag rockfall funnelled from the cliffs on both sides and heavy sluffing once the sun gets on it — one describes the lower section as potentially 'a bit of a garbage chute'. This is an early-start, frozen-conditions objective.

Both counts are the same descent with a different rope setup, not a disagreement. One published account: "5 rappels will get you down the route climbed and a 60M rope is long enough." The three stations listed are the two-rope sequence described elsewhere — a 60 m rappel to the belay atop pitch 2, then an overhanging double-rope rappel to just below Gunsight Notch. The stations total about 140 m of descent, which is ~5 rappels once a 60 m rope is doubled to 30.

From the Barlow Pass Trailhead (end of the paved Mountain Loop Highway drive), the approach is in two clearly different stages before you ever leave a maintained tread. Stage one is 4 flat, easy miles up the gated, washed-out Monte Cristo Road along the South Fork Sauk River to the Monte Cristo ghost town (~2,800 ft) — a couple of cable/suspension bridges cross the river en route, and this stretch is runnable/bikeable in dry conditions. At the townsite, walk past the old cabins, cross the bridge over 76 Creek, and follow "Dumas Street" through the settlement to pick up signed Glacier Basin Trail #719. Stage two is the real climb: the first half-mile follows an old mining road grade along Glacier Creek, then the trail turns into what regular hikers describe as 'more of a slick rock scramble than a hike' — steep, eroded, hands-on-rock terrain climbing past Glacier Falls, with numerous cascades and slick, root-braided rock steps that are notably harder (and slicker) descending than ascending. The trail crosses into Henry M. Jackson Wilderness and skirts the northeast edge of Mystery Hill before leveling out into Glacier Basin (~4,500 ft) after about 2.5 miles and ~1,700 ft of gain from Monte Cristo — roughly 6.5 miles and ~2,100 ft from the car. Glacier Creek parallels the whole climb and is a reliable water source, but it drains historic mine workings — treat/filter and be aware of elevated arsenic/heavy-metal readings noted by the Forest Service, especially in the lower reaches near the old townsite. From Glacier Basin the maintained trail ends; leave it and climb open talus and (typically) persistent steep snow — up to ~45° for a few hundred vertical feet — directly toward the obvious North Col (~6,760+ ft) on Monte Cristo's north ridge, with the Wilmans Peaks and Wilmans Glacier looming close overhead to climber's right. An ice axe and comfort on steep firm snow are essentially mandatory into midsummer; a moat can open at the col and the step across it can be intimidating or, late season, impassable. From the North Col, contour south (skier's/climber's left) across snow or talus below the summit cliffs, scouting for the obvious break/gully in the rock that gives the easiest way up to the base of the short summit chimney.

before.peakTraffic: Late May-June weekends, while the snow finger to Flypaper Pass is still intact and the approach road/trail season is opening up
before.estimatePerSeason: Low - likely well under 50 climbing parties per season (not precisely documented). Trip reports are mixed: one party saw no one else all day near the summit and called it 'a beautiful place without crowds,' while another noted a dozen-plus cars at the Dosewallips Road washout trailhead - but that trailhead is shared with the much more heavily used Anderson Pass/Enchanted Valley backpacking corridor, so most of that traffic is not headed for the glacier route.

before: Drive to the Crater Creek Trailhead (4,750 ft, 48.2205 / -120.26801). From Twisp take SR 20 south 2 miles to the SR 153 junction, then SR 153 south about 12 miles to County Road 1029 and on to CR 1034 (Gold Creek Road). CR 1034 becomes Forest Road 4340 after roughly 5 miles; continue about 1.6 miles further on FR 4340, then turn onto FR 4340-300 (Crater Creek Road) and follow it 4.6 miles to the trailhead. An alternate description of the same drive starts from Carlton: south on SR 153 for 3.5 miles, right on Gold Creek Loop Road 1.6 miles, right on Gold Creek Road 5.0 miles (becomes FR 4340), 1.6 miles more, then left on FR 4340-300 for 4.4 miles. The gravel is washboarded in places — drive it slowly. From the trailhead take Eagle Lakes Trail #431. The first 0.7 mile climbs gently, rounds a bend into an opening with a view up the Eagle Creek valley, then descends slightly to the bridge over Crater Creek. From there the trail climbs at a consistently gentle grade through mature pine into subalpine fir and larch. At roughly 5 miles the trail reaches the Eagle Lakes area and forks: take the right fork toward Upper Eagle Lake (7,115 ft, 48.213553 / -120.346815, about 6.2 trail miles and 2,350–2,430 ft of gain from the car). Upper Eagle Lake has many campsites and a large horse camp, and is the last reliable water. From the lake, the East Face of Bigelow is the wall directly above to the northwest — bear northwest up talus and heather to the base of the golden granite, roughly 0.4–0.5 mile and 900–1,000 ft above the lake. The FA party logged the whole thing as '8 miles more or less from TH, ~3500' to base' and called it a great, fast trail. Scout the line from the lake and from the base before racking up; the crack systems are genuinely hard to read from below.

before.cal: Best climbed June-Sept once the Chilliwack River fords and Challenger/Whatcom Glaciers are in reasonable shape; the Ross Lake Resort water taxi (used for the Beaver Pass variant) requires advance reservations.

days.note: From the Hannegan Pass trailhead, climb to Hannegan Pass (~5,000 ft), then drop roughly 2,500 ft into the Chilliwack River valley before re-climbing to camp at Whatcom Pass. Long day with a loaded pack on a mostly good trail; the up-down profile makes it feel longer than the raw mileage suggests.
days.title: Approach to Whatcom Pass camp
days.objective: Reach Whatcom Pass high camp (5,200 ft)

days.note: An early alpine start traverses below Whatcom Peak (dipping to ~5,300 ft) to Perfect Pass, then climbs the Challenger Glacier, crosses the bergschrund, and finishes with a short 5.5-5.7 rock pitch to the true summit. Round trip from camp runs about 11 hours including a lunch break.
days.title: Summit day via Perfect Pass and the Challenger Glacier

schedule.label: Leave Whatcom Pass camp
schedule.detail: Traverse toward Perfect Pass, dipping below Whatcom Peak.

schedule.label: Reach Perfect Pass
schedule.detail: 6,300 ft; roughly 3 hours from camp, one of the best bivy sites in the range.

schedule.label: Top out on the summit rocks
schedule.detail: Glacier ascent, bergschrund crossing, then a single 5.5-5.7 pitch (fixed gear) to the true summit.

schedule.label: Back to Perfect Pass
schedule.detail: Includes a lunch/rest break on the descent.

schedule.label: Return to Whatcom Pass camp
schedule.detail: About 11 hours car-to-camp round trip.

days.objective: Climb Mount Challenger via the Northwest (Challenger) Glacier

days.note: Reverse the approach over Hannegan Pass and back down to the car. Parties commonly treat this as a full day given the up-and-down profile; many build in a spare contingency day beforehand for weather given how remote and glacier-dependent this route is.
days.title: Exit to trailhead
days.objective: Hike back out to the Hannegan Pass trailhead

before.totalNote: "A remote 3-day trip (parties often pad in a 4th weather/contingency day): roughly 37 miles and ~10,000 ft of cumulative gain round trip, anchored by an 11-hour glacier summit day out of Whatcom Pass camp."

before.name: Dosewallips Road washout parking
before.note: "Same Dosewallips Road / Lake Constance approach as the other Constance routes, diverging higher up at Crystal Pass."

before: Mount Custer is a high, glaciated summit on the international border ridge near Mount Spickard and Mount Rahm, deep in the remote Chilliwack zone of North Cascades National Park. It's named for Henry Custer, a topographer who surveyed the US-Canada boundary through this area in the 1850s. The peak sits within an old volcanic caldera and is infamous for exceptionally loose, fractured, oxidized volcanic breccia — climbers commonly nickname it "Chosster," and one summit register was described as reading simply "horrible" regarding the rock. Two small glaciers (Custer Glacier, higher, and the larger Maselpanik Glacier lower in the cirque) mantle the north side, but the standard South Side route described here stays on rock, scree, and snow rather than glacier ice. First recorded ascent 1958 (Frank Dawe, Roy Mason, Karl Teichman).

before.optimalWindow: Mid-July through early September; mid-July to mid-August tends to offer the most consolidated approach snow and the most stable weather window

July.reason: Early July can still have lingering snow on approach slopes; conditions generally firm up and match the optimum by mid-month

June.reason: Snowbound in spring: approach and basin are typically still holding deep, unconsolidated snow with limited access

August.reason: Core of the best season - most consolidated snow, driest rock, and most stable alpine weather

September.reason: Still within the season window, but early fall storms and cooling temperatures ('fall: cold and stormy') can begin affecting conditions, especially late in the month

before: USFS lists the upper trailhead and access road as open 'early summer through fall' (roughly June–October); the lower, fee-free trailhead can often be reached earlier in spring. The snow chute is a classic glissade objective April–June while it still holds continuous snow — check NWAC advisories and recent trip reports, since the chute is an avalanche funnel that gets sun-baked by early-mid afternoon.
Described as 'a fairly easy scramble... ideal objective for beginner mountaineers' via Royal Basin/Constance Pass approaches. No rope or rack needed under normal conditions.

A standard alpine trad rack plus snow gear. The published short version is 'trad rack, picket or two'. In practice: a set of nuts, cams from small to about 2-3 inches, a few pitons are worth considering given the reported difficulty of finding solid placements, plenty of runners for wandering pitches, double ropes or a single 60 m plus a tag line for retreat, one or two pickets, and steel crampons and an ice axe (a second tool is worth having for the steeper snow). Rock shoes are worth carrying for the 5.9 crux - the route involves repeated snow-to-rock transitions, so a light pair pays for itself.

weather.typical: Remote North Cascades alpine, glaciated terrain
weather.probability: Convective/afternoon weather risk typical of high Cascades summer alpine terrain; more consequential here given the added steeper-ice terrain

before.exposure: Higher consequence than the standard routes: steeper ice climbing above glaciated terrain plus the same long, committing approach with limited bail options

avalanche.zone: Nearest NWAC coverage is West Slopes North, but this route is climbed entirely outside NWAC's Nov-Apr forecast season, so no direct zone forecast applies

before.crevasses: Present, with steeper ice sections in addition to standard crevasse/bergschrund hazard — "steeper ice steps" beyond what the Banded Glacier route requires

before: NPS explicitly warns not to depend on a cell phone in Olympic National Park backcountry — coverage is described as "very patchy throughout most of the park." This deep-interior route should be treated as having no reliable cell service; leave a detailed itinerary with someone before departing.
Objective hazards from Thumb Rock itself and rock bands above at 10,500 ft bivy area
Active avalanche discharge documented: 'Avalanche from Willis Wall' photo evidence of active snow sloughs from adjacent terrain
Vertical ice pitches at bergschrund crossing (5-8 ft sections)
Optional short 70-80 degree ice pitch through the rock band just above Thumb Rock - the usual line goes around it on the left
Sustained 40-60 degree ice climbing approaching Liberty Cap Glacier
50-60 degree steep snow/ice faces on east ridge above Black Pyramid
Seasonal bridges and icy ledges require careful crevasse navigation
Intricate Carbon Glacier crossing - complex crevasse systems throughout
Extreme wind exposure at altitude: documented 80mph summit winds
Grade IV route - serious alpine undertaking requiring solid ice climbing and glacier travel skills

Descend by reversing the ascent line: down the summit scree/rock to the saddle, then back along the boot path traverse across scree/grass/rock benches around the south and east flanks to the 5,800-ft saddle above Lake of the Angels, down to the lake, and out the Putvin Trail to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb - there is no rappelling anywhere on the standard scramble route. The main descent hazard is the same rotten rock and loose scree that makes the ascent tricky: downclimbing the exposed class 3 sections near the summit ridge crest is generally regarded as harder and more hazard-prone than climbing them, and parties should stay well left/south of the steeper cliffy drop-off noted on the north side of the upper mountain (parties specifically warn that contouring too far right/north near the ridge crest 'gets sketchy, exposed, and dangerous' and to cut west over the ridge instead). Watch for rockfall onto climbers below on the scree/talus sections, expect residual snow in the gullies and on the traverse into early summer (ice axe/crampons may be warranted), and budget real time for careful downclimbing rather than assuming a fast glissade-style descent - one party logged about 2.5 hours from summit back to the trailhead, but that was in good, snow-free conditions.

On August 19, 2006, Blake Herrington and Tim Haider left the Agnes Creek Trail at Swamp Creek and climbed Needle Peak via its North Ridge, then continued along the connecting ridgeline, making the first ascents of the North and South Anonymity Towers, before climbing the Dark Glacier to a bivouac atop Dark Peak. The next day they continued the ridge crest to Bonanza Peak's west and main summits. The overall linkup was rated Grade V, 5.8, and described as 'wild and highly variable in quality' along the crest; the source account does not break the grade, pitch count, or length out separately for the Needle Peak segment alone.

Molar Tooth North Ridge/West Side: low 5th class terrain with complex route-finding and exposure; 'if you were to lead this you may not find much pro.' Descent via 3 rappels off the north ridge — some fixed anchors present but sparse traffic means bring gear to replace old tat.

weather.typical: Summers relatively dry/clear; the range is otherwise cloudy and wet, which would sharply increase rockfall/routefinding risk if encountered mid-climb

before.exposure: Grade IV, sustained, remote terrain with a difficult descent (Doug's Direct or the C-J Couloir); bail-out options are poor once committed

avalanche.zone: Mountain 'frequently looses enormous avalanches' from several hanging glaciers per route descriptions; maritime snowpack is wet and heavy, elevating hazard especially outside the stable summer window

crevasses.timing: Steep snow sections (45–60°) on approach/descent carry real fall consequence; most hazardous outside the summer stable window
crevasses.location: Route crosses beneath/adjacent to a hanging glacier and the Sill Glacier

before: A light alpine rock rack weighted toward small-to-mid cams (roughly 0.3-2in) and a modest nut set — the first-ascent account describes the rock as 'the consistency of feta cheese' and the crux as two pitches of a-cheval straddling a crumbling ridge crest, meaning placements will be scarce and often marginal rather than plentiful. This is not a route to bring a full double rack for; prioritize a few bomber pieces you can trust over volume. Given the X rating (runout/poor pro), extra cordage/slings for improvised anchors off horns, chockstones, or rock features is worth the weight, since natural gear placements can't be counted on.

Painted Mountain (also historically called Red Mountain) is a distinctive red/orange, mineral-streaked 6,975 ft summit in the western Glacier Peak Wilderness, roughly 17-20 miles southeast of Darrington via the Mountain Loop Highway. Its Lushootseed name, 'Ska-hala-bats' ('painted'), was recorded by early Forest Service ranger Nels Bruseth; USGS surveyor Sam Strom had earlier dubbed it 'Red Mountain,' and 'Painted Mountain' became the official name in 1981 via the U.S. Board on Geographic Names. A fire lookout (1936-1967) once stood on a bench about a mile up the trail at roughly 2,800 ft, far below the summit, part of the dense North Cascades lookout network of the early-to-mid 1900s, and the peak was likely first climbed around 1897 by a USGS survey party. The mountain is built of Late Cretaceous migmatitic gneiss whose oxidized reddish-orange bands give it its name and its 'huge massif of red rocks' summit block.

before.name: SR-20 Wine Spires pullout / Burgundy Col climbers' trail
before.directions: Park at the roadside pullout on SR-20, about seven-tenths of a mile past the Cutthroat Lake Road turnoff and directly across the highway from the Wine Spires. The boot and climbers' trail for Burgundy Col begins right at this pullout, dropping off the road shoulder.

before.name: Burgundy Col
before.note: "7,770-ft notch separating the Wine Spires from Vasiliki Ridge, reached via steep talus/scree above the Bench camp."
before.directions: From the pullout a boot/climbers' trail drops off the shoulder, crosses Early Winters Creek on logs or a rock-hop (a wet ford in early-season snowmelt), and climbs a timbered rib on the climber's-left side of the Burgundy Creek drainage, gaining about 2,000 ft over the first 1.5-2 miles to a broad flat bench at 6,400-6,600 ft. The bench is the last reliable water and can run dry by late summer; above it the trail continues up steep talus and scree to the col.

before.name: Pernod Spire Summit
before.directions: From Burgundy Col, cross to the east side and traverse south below the east walls, then climb obliquely up to the notch between Pernod and Chianti; from the notch the line goes up the northeast corner to the small summit block, which carries old first-ascent bolts worth backing up.

before: From the top, traverse the summit ridge of the Blob northward toward the Blob/Terror col — described by the first-ascent party as "an adventure in itself," with short simul-climbing recommended over the exposed crest. At the col edge, locate webbing rappel anchors over a steep step and make two rappels down into the notch. From the notch, an easy scramble down the col returns climbers to the bench below.

A steep, continuous four-pitch corner line right of the West Ridge. The route is described as "pretty mellow for a 5.10" on alpine rock: the pitch 2 and pitch 3 cruxes (a roof with fingerlocks, then flaring finger/hand jams) are short-lived, and the climbing stays clean and well-featured throughout. Often combined with a route on Burgundy Spire's North Face for a longer link-up day.

weather.typical: North Cascades maritime alpine weather — cool and often cloudy/wet even in the summer window; best conditions come during multi-day stable high-pressure stretches
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms are a recognized hazard on the exposed summit block and open glacier terrain, especially on warm July-August afternoons

before.exposure: Consequential — an 'exposed Class 4 summit block' with real fall consequences at the top, on top of standard glacier crevasse-fall exposure during the approach and climb

avalanche.zone: No NWAC zone/product specifically covers this peak, and NWAC's published avalanche forecast season does not extend into the Jul-Sep climbing window for this route — treat as a data gap rather than a zero-risk claim

before.crevasses: Significant — the Colonial and Neve Glaciers have real, open crevasses, with crevasse fall on the Neve Glacier the hazard; the glacier is reportedly well-bridged early season but opens up notably after mid-July, at which point the direct line below Paul Bunyan's Stump becomes unsafe and parties detour via the rock rib on the SE side of the basin

before: Verified beta: 'standard glacier gear, rock pro to 2.5 inches.' Route climbs the 400ft 'Great Gash' corner/chimney system; descent via the West Ridge (rappels).

before.name: Depot Creek Road parking / trailhead
before.note: "Standard Depot Creek/Chilliwack Lake Road (Canada) trailhead for Mox Peaks/Redoubt approaches, via Depot Creek Falls and Ouzel Lake."
before.directions: This trailhead is on the Canadian side of the border: follow Chilliwack Lake Road in BC to the abandoned logging spur at Depot Creek, where the parking sits at roughly 2,350 ft. From there the approach walks the old roadway grade, taking the left-hand fork, about a mile to the Monument 65 border marker, where you cross into North Cascades National Park and should sign in at the wilderness-permit kiosk.

before.name: Monument 65 (US-Canada border)
before.note: Border obelisk and North Cascades NP trail register/kiosk in old growth ~200 yd past the parking intersection; register for backcountry entry here.

before.name: Depot Creek Falls handline/cable step
before.note: Class 3 scramble past a ~967-ft waterfall on wet, slippery rock; an old cable/handline aids a steep, misty 8-ft rock step.

before.name: Ouzel Lake camp
before.note: Flat sandy/gravelly moraine benches above the lake outlet; established high-camp for Chilliwack-range climbs, ~9+ hrs / 3,550 ft above the cars.

before.name: Redoubt Glacier saddle / high camp
before.note: Broken buttress SW of Ouzel Lake tops out on rock outcrops at this glacier-edge saddle; rope up here for crevassed glacier travel, visibility often poor.

before.name: Col of the Wild
before.note: Contour ~2 mi of moderately steep snow on the Redoubt Glacier to this col between the Mox Peaks; final ~100 ft is loose talus over sand.

before.name: Gendarme notch below SE Mox
before.note: Class 2-3 ledges and a Class 4 headwall gain the high notch on the west side of the summit tower; rock is notably loose with high exposure.

before.name: Southeast Mox Peak (Hard Mox) summit
before.note: Three pitches up to 5.5 (mostly Class 3-4 on the final pitch) above the notch to the true summit; descend by downclimbing/short-rappelling back to the notch.

before: Start at the Hannegan Pass Trailhead (elev. ~3,120 ft) at the end of Ruth Creek Road (FS-32). From the trailhead, follow the maintained Hannegan Pass Trail #674 gently up the Ruth Creek valley (views of Mt. Sefrit and Nooksack Ridge) for about 4 miles and roughly 2,000 ft of gain to 5,050 ft Hannegan Pass — this stretch is straightforward, well-graded, and has reliable water at Ruth Creek crossings for the first couple of miles. From the pass, stay on the maintained trail as it drops past Boundary Camp and Copper Creek Camp into the Chilliwack valley; roughly two miles beyond Copper Creek an easily missed side path leads down to the Chilliwack River ford (about 2,750 ft), and the Easy Ridge path climbs steeply from the far bank. From here it is sustained, largely cross-country travel: climb onto and follow Easy Ridge itself, a hot, dry, open, south-facing ridge crest with limited shade — flowing water is available relatively early on the ridge but the FA party warned this stretch 'would be brutal later in the season and in dry years.' Continue along/over Easy Peak (a common first bivy, roughly a full day, ~10 hours, from the trailhead) and then descend/traverse past the notch known as Imperfect Impasse, before regaining elevation to Challenger Col on the flank of Mt. Challenger. From Challenger Col, traverse the southern Challenger cirque (glacial terrain — rope/crevasse-awareness recommended near the pocket glacier) toward the west ridge of Phantom Peak, a typical second bivy site, avoiding lingering snow at Pickle Pass. From this high camp it is a further, mostly straightforward cross-country traverse across the western slopes to the base of Spectre Peak's south ridge, reached around sunrise on what is effectively day three. In total this is roughly a 46-mile, ~17,500 ft round-trip approach-and-climb outing (74 km), typically broken into 2 or more travel days each way with route-finding, glacier travel, and off-trail ridge scrambling throughout — this is genuinely one of the longest, most remote approaches in the North Cascades, not a simple hike-in.

before.notes: Leaving the moat/talus at the toe of the East Face, the route starts up broken, blocky slab low on the wall; gear is spaced over lichen-covered rock as the line establishes itself above the approach.
Continued low-angle slab climbing on compact but featured rock; short discontinuous crack systems are linked with smeared friction moves.
An easier ramp/traverse picks the path of least resistance across a brushy, broken slab shelf, part of the extensive route-finding the FA party described on the lower wall.
The slab steepens; thin, discontinuous cracks are taken with small cams and nuts, with natural protection sparse and spaced.
A long run-out friction-slab pitch, the kind of ground the FA account describes covering efficiently (with simul-climbing) low on the 1,000-ft slab section beneath the headwall.
A short, steeper bulge breaks up the slab; positive edges allow pulling over onto easier ground above.
Moderate slab climbing resumes, weaving around loose blocks and lichen-covered patches typical of this remote, rarely-traveled face.
A steeper corner/crack splits the slab here; stemming and jamming past a small bulge is the crux move of the lower wall.
Slab climbing eases as the angle transitions toward the base of the headwall proper; broken ledges and ramps link the pitch together.
A short final pitch gains the small stance/bivy ledge at roughly 1,000 ft up the face, at the base of the 1,500-ft headwall, where the FA party (Layton/Wolfe, 2005) spent their one night out.
Leaving the bivy ledge, the headwall begins in earnest on a steep crack system; the rock here is noticeably more compact than the slabs below, though protection stays sparse.
Sustained crack and face climbing up the lower headwall, small cams and stoppers in a discontinuous crack; the wall's angle is now consistently steep.
A short, steep section past a bulge/mini-roof on face holds; gear thins out noticeably above the lip.

A corner system provides the natural line here; stemming and liebacking with protection that is adequate but spaced, consistent with the loose, poorly-protected character the FA team described of the wall overall.
Technical face climbing links small edges past a blank-looking section; noticeably harder than anything below and a preview of the difficulty concentrating higher on the headwall.
Continued corner and crack climbing higher on the headwall, with exposure mounting as the face steepens further toward vertical.
A strenuous crack pitch, hands to fists through a discontinuous system, with gear sparse but adequate for a committed leader.
