Face climbing on knobs and edges links two crack systems; rock quality remains loose in places, matching the FA account's description of 'steep, loose and poorly protected rock' through the headwall.
A steep face pitch on small wires and cams placed in shallow seams; the climbing is technical and increasingly run-out between placements.
The headwall steepens toward vertical as the party enters the upper third of the route; thin, technical climbing on marginal protection.

A traversing pitch searching out the line of weakness in an increasingly blank upper headwall, reflecting the real route-finding uncertainty the FA party described forcing their way through near the top.
A short, steep pitch gains a cramped stance below the final overhangs; belays through here are hanging or semi-hanging, built entirely from natural gear.
Sustained, strenuous climbing directly below the crux; rock quality improves slightly here but protection is still sparse ahead of the route's hardest moves.

The documented crux: the FA account describes surmounting the 'final overhangs' on this pitch with the leader unable to see where the next piece of protection would be. First climbed with a short aid section (recorded as 5.9+ A2-), later free ascents rate it around 5.11-; treat the X rating as literal on a route this remote.

An easy final pitch over loose, 'sandy blocks of stacked garbage' tops out the East Face. The FA party (Layton/Wolfe) stopped here rather than continuing to Hard Mox's true summit, out of food and water, marking their high point with a playing card before beginning the rappel descent.

before: Two different descents are described for this route, and they are not the same line. The standard walk-off IS available to parties who climbed The Scoop — one party did exactly that: “Make a 30m rappel to east from slung horn, then scramble down scree or snow rightward and back to the base of the climb.” The first-ascent report notes the route “can be rappelled with two 60m ropes, to avoid the loose descent” and that they left “only natural anchors for the descent”, but publishes no station count, so none is given here.

Two real options, and most parties take the walk-off. Option 1 (walk-off): from the East Shoulder, make an exposed, somewhat sketchy 4th-class traverse west (it borders on unprotected 5th-class slab in spots, so many parties stay roped) to gain the same descent gully used off the East Face. Downclimb the gully, then traverse north (right) to pick up the climbers'/cattle trail that runs up to Liberty Bell, which drops you onto the Blue Lake Trail; a faint climbers' path cuts off a final stretch of trail before the highway. Option 2 (rappel the route): from the top, the first anchor is a bolted station roughly 20-30 feet above the old P6 slung-block anchor. With double 70m ropes (a 70m lead line plus a 70m tag line) you can rappel from the very top of the route; doubled 60m ropes will not reach that first station. If you're bailing from above the P5 crux rather than finishing the route, two 60m ropes are workable using a fixed nut-and-sling anchor partway down P6 as an intermediate station — anything shorter risks coming up short between anchors. Lower down, rappel stations are described as "obvious, good-quality anchors" on trees or bolts. Hardware is mixed vintage: some original 1989 5/16" bolts remain despite a post-2016 rebolting push, and at least one older fixed-nut/sling anchor is noted as aging — back up or inspect any anchor you didn't place yourself before weighting it.

requiredSkills: Genuine glacier travel/crampon skill for the Stuart Glacier crossing — one party found traction devices inadequate even in August since it is a permanent glacier remnant
before.experienceLevel: Solid 5.9 trad leading while fatigued, after ~11 pitches of moderate rock leading into 2 crux 5.9 pitches ('1,000 ft of exposure')

before.notes: Two starts. The better one drops by an exposed 3rd-class traverse around the toe of the buttress to a clean layback flake, then a low-angle groove to 3rd-class slabs. The original start scrambles a gully over a large flake-chockstone. Either way, traverse hard right along a grassy ledge system to a gear belay below the faint white dike splitting the slab. This rightward jog is where parties most often go off route.

Climb the thin white dike past three bolts to a narrow ledge, then traverse right and up a short gully to a fixed anchor on the skyline. Some parties rate this slab the crux of the route. Keep slings long on the traverse to manage rope drag, and watch for parties above in the gully.

Step right, then traverse left on positive edges toward the skyline past bolt protection. Go up the arête past old fixed pins through a short, fun dihedral, and belay on gear at a heather ledge. Back up the old pins rather than trusting them alone.

Climb steep stacked blocks, then easier zig-zag cracks to a fixed anchor. Loose rock is the hazard here: a large detached block sits on this ground and can take away gear options. Test holds, keep the rope off loose edges, and keep the belayer out of the fall line.

Often called the crux: an airy face traverse out along the ragged east edge of the north face. Pass two bolts, then traverse right about 50 ft to a fixed anchor on the skyline. The exposure is big but the rock takes gear well. Protect the traverse for the follower as well as the leader.

The finish: a long, easy romp up the arête to a last bit of heather and the summit, where there is a bolted anchor. From the top, walk off the southeast side to rejoin the standard route. No rappels are needed.

before: Accounts disagree on the count. A Mountaineers trip report has “the team rappelled three times on the way down”; another party “rappelled twice from the top of the keyhole to reach the bottom”. A third account describes five rappels, but that is one party’s descent on two 25 m ropes rather than a list of fixed stations — which is why its lengths (about 23 m / 75 ft) look so precise and why its count disagrees with the others. That party’s final rappel off the southeast rib jammed and they sacrificed a rope; the standard line threads the low keyhole beneath the chockstone for a cleaner pull.

Published descriptions give the rack simply as 'a light rack of nuts and long slings' for this Grade II, 5.5, 5-7 pitch ridge route (pitch count varies with line chosen). Terrain includes sections of loose boulders.

A short, moderate 2-3 pitch rock climb up 'very moderate rock scrambling' culminating in the 'infamous chockstone chimney,' rated 5.2 and about 60 ft long. Reached after a long approach and glacier traverse; can be descended by rappelling the route or by continuing on a loop past nearby summits.

No exact cam-by-cam list is documented for this specific route, so the rack below is a reasoned inference from route character: unusually hard rock (the first-ascent account describes it only as "unusually hard rock" with piton cracks that "virtually disappear" higher up — a 2013 trip report informally nicknames it "Rhino Stone" but gives no mineral composition, so it should not be assumed to be granodiorite, rhyolite, or any other named rock type), a single ~5.10c crux headwall pitch, with the rest of the roughly 1000ft of technical climbing more moderate (5.6-5.9). A single alpine rack from small nuts through 3in cams, doubled in the 0.5-1.5in hand/finger range.

before.pull: A rope end has jammed in a crack on the right side of this rappel, forcing the party to climb back up the other strand to free it - and the ground you would climb to reach it is loose. Watch where the ends land and pull away from the crack.
before.notes: First rappel off the shared summit down to the P7 anchor on Mile High Club's line; single 60m rope reaches comfortably.
before.anchor: summit rap rings, station ~8ft south of summit bolts and ~4ft off the ground
hazards: The edge below this station has cut a rope badly enough that the party had to chop it in half and retire it. The route page says the edge has since been ground down; the Beyond Redlining page still tells you exactly where to lay the rope, so treat it as live

A hard pendulum. The first-ascent advice is to lower to the large flake and walk left to the belay rather than rappelling free; a 2025 party swung hard right into a separate rock face on this rappel, on both of their visits
The nuts on these rap rings have been found loose - check them before you weight the station

Rappelling Beyond Redlining's own line is what this station exists to avoid: its first pitch is over 50 m, several pitches angle substantially left or right, and it needs angling rappels off single bolts, many of which only reach the next anchor on rope stretch
before.station: Not on Beyond Redlining. From the shared summit, walk about 50 ft over to Mile High Club's top station: the rap rings are set back from the top of the route, and the place to lay the rope is the least sharp part of the edge roughly 8 ft south of the bolts and about 4 ft off the ground. Toss just left of the crest, then angle down to the lower anchor at the base of pitch 7. From here the whole descent stays about 10-15 ft skier's left of the bolt line, and for most pitches you can see the climbing anchors from the rap anchors.

before.notes: A face-descent rappel down to the P6 anchor.
hazards: Dropping to the dihedral-top anchor instead is a specific, named mistake - the station you want is above and left of it
The published reason for tossing left is that parties climb directly below: keep the rope and anything you knock loose off them
before.station: Toss the rope slightly left of the bolt line rather than straight down. Rappel the pitch-6 face, then move to a rap anchor about 10 ft skier's left and 10 ft above the anchor at the top of the dihedral pitch. Do not continue to the top of the dihedral pitch.

before.notes: A short rappel down to a ledge at P5; source explicitly flags this one as short.
hazards: Free-hanging above a ledge, so you arrive spinning onto a stance rather than sliding onto it
before.station: A short rappel from the pitch-5 station to an anchor on a ledge off to the side of the dihedral pitch. It is free-hanging above the ledge.

before.notes: Drops to P4, where one of two available anchor options is used.
hazards: Most stations on this route have two anchors a few feet apart so ascending and descending parties do not share one - taking the wrong one puts you on top of climbers
Rope thrown from here lands on anyone on pitch 4 below
before.station: Two anchors are available here; take the skier's-left one where you can, which keeps you off the climbing line.

before.pull: A rope has been stuck in a crack pulling from the pitch-3 rap anchors; pull away from the crack. Feed the rope through the cedar bushes rather than throwing it.
before.notes: The most commonly botched rappel on the descent — aim for a 10-ft-tall tree roughly 15 ft skier's-left of the climbing line; a hidden intermediate anchor is tucked in cedar bushes just below the visible upper-P3 station.
hazards: The route page states it outright: do not rappel down the vertical face on a single rope, because you will not reach the next anchors. Parties who miss it end up either doing two double-rope rappels from the top of pitch 3 or, on an 80 m, nearly reaching the pitch-2 anchors and then having to scramble across exposed ground
One party that missed it could not retrieve their rope at all - the pull angle around the intervening features made it stick and recovering it was judged unsafe
The tree the beta says will be flagged has never been flagged; it is still described as 'we will flag this tree soon' years later
before.station: The confusing one, and by a wide margin the most-reported problem on this descent. From the pitch-4 anchor, pass through cedar bushes directly below the station and rappel the low-angle upper part of pitch 3 - it is mostly walking. Aim for a tree about 10 ft tall standing roughly 15 ft skier's left of the climbing line; the intermediate anchor is tucked into a nook just below that tree. Look for it right where the ground turns from slabby to vertical. You cannot see this anchor on the way up, so it cannot be scouted on the climb; parties have found chalk arrows pointing at it.

before.notes: Continues down to a lower-P3 anchor, landing on a large ledge.
hazards: This is the vertical face the station above exists to get you onto safely; it is the ground you would be stranded above having missed the nook
before.station: From the nook anchor, rappel the vertical section at the start of pitch 3 down to a large ledge, and set up at either of the anchors at the top of pitch 2 - the skier's-left one if it is free.

before.notes: Drops to the P2 anchor.
hazards: Parties consistently record being surprised that the last anchor before the ground is a separate one, offset from the climbing anchor
before.station: The station is NOT the pitch-1 climbing anchor, which is what people expect and head for. The rap anchor is about 10 ft down and 10-15 ft skier's left of the pitch-1 belay anchor.

before.pull: Consider staying on rappel and walking back to the belay bolt at the start of the route, then pulling the rope from there.
before.notes: Final rappel(s) via the P2 and P1 anchors bring you to the base of the route.
hazards: Do not treat the base of the route as the ground - the ledge you land on is exposed and hundreds of feet up
The gully to climber's right throws natural rockfall onto the start of the scramble; keep helmets on until you are clear of it, especially with parties above
before.station: Final rappel to the base of the route. The starting ledge is several hundred feet above the ground and quite exposed.

before: The crux lead is described as following 'a very sharp crest' — expect sustained exposure on both sides near the top of the class 5 section

Roughly June through August. Early enough in that window for the CJ Couloir to still hold consolidated snow/neve for a safer up-and-down (it gets more broken up and rockier as the season goes on), but late enough for the NW Chimney's rock pitches to be dry. A late-July (7/27) ascent found the couloir 'not that steep till the last few hundred feet' and mostly moderate two-tool climbing, per a 2013 trip report.

Follows "a series of seams up the center of the steep main face": thin boulder climbing up a steep wall to a small overhang, then a few big moves on good holds before easier terrain and the anchors, which are shared with the adjacent Firearms.

July.reason: Prime dry-rock conditions ("Prime; afternoon storm risk")

June.reason: Season technically opens late June, but the approach gully can still hold snow in a heavy snow year

August.reason: Height of summer dry season; watch for afternoon storms

October.reason: Beyond the season window; SR 20 closes seasonally and early snow becomes likely

September.reason: Cooler with shorter days but generally stable

before:
Almost all the difficulty here is brush, steepness and route-finding rather than climbing. The rock is rated Class 4, but that grade comes from a climber who climbed it in January and has been honest about the limits of that experience — he can only guess at the difficulty of the rock and the number of pitches, if any, because good snow may have covered the harder steps.

From the Gorge Creek bridge at 1,096 ft the slope is sustained from the first step, gaining roughly 1,800 ft in the first half mile through small evergreens with a salal and brush understory. There is no trail, and numerous rock outcrops make navigation important. One recorded line: from near the highway curve, hike due north to about 2,800 ft, turn northeast and ascend to the 4,920+ ft point, then go straight uphill on a bearing of about 340 degrees true to Point 5872, where the south ridge becomes obvious. A party approaching via Gorge Creek instead took the South Buttress, turning cliff bands at about 2,400 ft and 2,800 ft on the right, moving through open timber and alpine snowfields, and reaching the South Davis saddle at 5,700 ft in 4.4 hours from the car; they described Class 2-3 scrambling on the buttress with slime-coated rock slabs near the top. A third account has the granite slabs starting around 4,850 ft after a brushy gully at 3,600 ft, bypassing Point 5872 to the north, and reaching a south-ridge viewpoint at 6,300 ft.

From the 5,720+ ft saddle, the instruction is to 'climb 200 ft of slab to the sharp ridge leading to the summit.' In good snow this is step-kicking; bare it is class 4 slab. In snow this is where the route's steepest ground is — the notch on the old standard south ridge line is reported at 65 degrees, which is precisely why skiers pushed a variation onto the southwest face. Above it the crest broadens into an almost level, wide-open ridge to the summit, one of the great walkable viewpoints in the range and simultaneously the top of the largest cornices most people will ever stand near. In summer that broad snow crest may instead be a scramble among rocks with steep drops on both sides.

There is also a variation that its climber did not rate: from the saddle, drop east into the basin under the east side of the south ridge, traverse up and north as far as possible, then turn west and climb beside the cliff edge. The turn involves a ten-foot step that looked trivial and was not — iced-in cracks and wrong-feeling holds, passed with ice-axe belays. His verdict on the direct ridge, descended on the return, was that it 'had all the ledges we needed to get down'. Take the ridge.

There is almost no descent-specific beta for Der Dihedral beyond the note that it 'joins the 1972 NE Arete to finish.' Since the route tops out on the same upper mountain terrain as Backbone Ridge, the standard descent is the same walk-off used for that route and for the summit generally: scramble/snow traverse southeast to a saddle, then east across the long snow slope to Aasgard Pass, and down the pass's steep talus/snow (~2,200 ft in under a mile) to Colchuck Lake, favoring climbers' left near the granite walls. Crampons/axe are worth carrying into mid-summer. A rappel alternative exists on Backbone Ridge's finish for icy conditions (ledges below the summit to a rap station, two rappels to a ledge system, then a scramble north to Aasgard Pass) - if Der Dihedral's top-out lands near that same station it may be usable, but this has not been confirmed for this route, so plan on the standard walk-off by default.

Full rack from small nuts/finger-size cams up through a BD #4 (~4in) — the #4 is specifically noted as 'helpful on the lower crux.' Bring doubles of the mid-range cams (roughly 0.4-2in) to cover sustained, varied crack sizes across the route's 21 pitches, including the P3 5.10- roof and the awkward P16a 5.10- offwidth (harder with a loaded pack).

Confirmed as Eldorado Peak's Main Peak North Ridge: climbs 'the path of least resistance on clean solid rock,' mostly the east side of the ridge, ending below the summit pinnacle; protection listed only as 'standard alpine pro.' Steep snow on the NE Face means glacier travel gear is needed for the approach/upper mountain in addition to the rock rack.

before.optimalWindow: Mid-July through September, consistent with prior research; late July into August is the most reliable stretch

July.reason: Early July can still hold lingering snow in shaded gullies; by mid-July the route enters its prime dry-rock window

June.reason: Snowbound in spring with limited access to the approach drainages; not a standard scramble window

August.reason: Peak of the prime summer window - driest rock and most stable access, though afternoon thunderstorms remain a recurring hazard

September.reason: Good conditions early in the month ("good early, deteriorating later"); increasing chance of early-season weather and shortening days later in the month

before: Forbidden's tallest, steepest, and most remote established route, first climbed by Fred Beckey and Ed Cooper in July 1959. Beckey called it 'an exceptional climb of purity' whose mixed character 'requires some genuine climbing and flexible alpine skills.' From a high bivy, roughly 500 ft of steep, somewhat loose 4th-to-low-5th-class terrain gains a knife-edge section (5.6), leading into four 60m pitches up to the 5.8 crux before the face blends into the upper West Ridge near the summit.

Four Brothers is a cluster of four rocky points on Chikamin Ridge. Reports on the adjacent, better-documented Chikamin Peak route describe the ridge-crest side of Four Brothers as presenting 'very difficult (and technical) obstacles,' and parties headed for Chikamin Peak deliberately detour around it via steep grassy slopes and gully systems well south of Chikamin Pass. The Southwest Route on Four Brothers itself follows this gentler southwest aspect rather than the ridge crest.

July through September, and only when bone dry. #2 Gully is polished and mossy on one side and pure sand-and-rubble on the other, and the whole route is dirt and vegetation — one climber's summary was 'woe be to anyone who tries this route when it is not bone dry'. Take the longest days of summer: the standard ascent runs 15+ hours.

Descend by reversing the ascent line: downclimb the south face/south arete/west-face traverse used on the first-ascent route back to the notch below the summit horn, then continue down snow/talus to the Luna Cirque camp at Luna or Lousy Lake. I could not find a trip report giving pitch-by-pitch rappel beta specific to Ghost Peak. Based on its character - a small, generally solid rock horn climbed by a 3rd/4th-class face-and-arete traverse, similar in scale to neighboring Pickets summits like Crooked Thumb and Phantom Peak - most parties simply downclimb the way they came, with no fixed or bolted anchors anywhere in this remote sub-range. Carry a rope and a small rack of slings/nuts in case the exposure or wet/icy rock make a short rappel preferable off a natural anchor (slung horn or chockstone) near the top of the arete; a single 30m rappel would be more than enough to protect the steepest section if needed. Treat this as a walk-off/downclimb route with a possible single natural-anchor rappel in reserve, not a route with a defined multi-rappel descent. Once back at camp, reverse the full approach: back over Pt. 7374 to Challenger Arm, over Perfect Pass/Whatcom Glacier or Whatcom Peak's north ridge to Whatcom Pass, then down the Brush Creek Trail, back across the Chilliwack River and over Hannegan Pass to the Hannegan trailhead.
Follow the white pyroclastic aggregate band specifically — it's described as solid and abrasive ('like a climbing wall') compared to the looser dark rock around it.
Hold a consistent traverse elevation (~7,500 ft) with your party to avoid knocking rock down onto teammates below.
Goat paths along the Goat Ribs/Goat Ledges are a useful route-finding aid.

"This route follows the large blocky groove between Just Enough and Notta Slab." Shares its start with Notta Slab, then breaks left into a wide, chimney-like feature after the 2nd bolt. 16 bolts to chain anchors; a 70m rope is needed to lower/toprope the full length, and walkers can also descend from the summit.
Crux is low; "holds should hold" per the route description — go up and through the shaded portion on the right.

From the Himmel-Otto (Himmelhorn-Ottohorn) col, scramble about 50 ft east until the terrain steepens to vertical and the route begins. Four pitches of crack and low-5th ridge scrambling lead to the summit block. John Roper, one of the first ascensionists, called it 'the best climb I've ever done in the North Cascades.'
A moderate, low-key alternative to the East Ridge and West Face — described by its first ascensionists as 'a fun day out.'
Approach and descent options overlap with the East Ridge route, so beta is easy to combine.

Confirmed as a 30ft (9m) single-pitch sport route in the Minidike sub-area of The Dikes, WA, described as 'bolts to anchors' and 'great for teaching new climbers.' 60m rope is far more than sufficient for a route this short.

before.name: North Fork Sauk Trailhead
before.note: End of FR 49 (6.4 mi off the Mountain Loop Hwy area); Northwest Forest Pass required and a self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the kiosk; start of North Fork Sauk Trail #649.

before.name: Pilot Ridge Trail junction
before.note: Trail #649 forks with Pilot Ridge Trail #652 here; stay on #649 (the lower, riverside route) toward Mackinaw Shelter.
before.directions: The first two miles are the gentlest of the trip: an easy grade through old-growth forest along the North Fork Sauk River, gaining only a few hundred feet.

before.name: Red Creek crossing
before.note: Ford Red Creek on the climbers' path; hikers describe it as 'interesting but not difficult' at normal flow, tougher during peak snowmelt.
before.directions: Two more nearly flat miles up the valley on good tread, crossing several small tributaries on the way. Red Creek is the first crossing that can actually stop you — it is manageable at normal flow but runs considerably higher during snowmelt or after heavy rain, and a pole or a sturdy stick helps with balance.

before.name: Mackinaw Shelter
before.note: Historic three-sided log shelter beside the North Fork Sauk River; the last easy, reliable camp before the trail turns steep and switchbacked toward White Pass.
before.directions: A last easy mile beside the river brings you to the shelter clearing. Flat ground here is limited and a larger party will find it tight. Fill water before moving on, because the trail leaves the river from this point.

before.name: White Pass (PCT junction)
before.note: Trail #649 tops out on the Pacific Crest Trail after ~3.2 steep miles from Mackinaw Shelter; broad meadow/basin here with camping and a view down into Foam Basin.
before.directions: The trail turns uphill in earnest and gains roughly 3,000 ft in sustained switchbacks through subalpine forest to a meadow junction with the Pacific Crest Trail, where Glacier Peak and the White Chuck side of the massif first come into view. Turn north on the PCT and follow it about a quarter mile to the pass. This is the last easy, reliable water before the high traverse.

before.name: Glacier Gap crevasse crossing
before.note: Crossing point between the White Chuck Glacier and White River Glacier near a tarn-dotted basin; crevasses open by late season here — rope up before continuing toward Kololo.
before.directions: The maintained trail ends here. Traverse north below the White Mountain ridge into Foam Basin and White River Meadows, the usual base camp, either by way of Red Pass or by crossing snowfields to the notch west of Point 6770 and dropping into the White Chuck basin. From camp climb to Foam Pass and cross the White Chuck Glacier to the gap — this is glacier travel on largely featureless snow, so carry a track or the navigation skill to retrace it in cloud, and be roped for the crevasses low on the glacier, which can be fully open.

before.name: Kololo Peaks (summit)
before.note: Summit gained by a short rock scramble off the White River Glacier after the final low-angle ice/snow pitch; of the twin tops a short walk apart, the eastern one is the true high point by 10-15 ft, so tag both.
before.directions: From the gap gain the flat shoulder at about 6,000 ft, then follow the connecting ridge north-northwest over a bulge near 7,200 ft, cross the small basin below the east summit, and continue west a quarter mile to a saddle at 7,400 ft. From the saddle, the ridge forming the east edge of the White River Glacier cirque leads to the final low-angle snow and a short talus-and-ledge scramble to the top. Expect a stretch of exposed blue ice a couple of hundred yards long on the White River Glacier — that section wants crampons and deliberate footwork rather than a plod.

before: This is the line described as a ridge that 'just screams skin me in winter'. In summer it is a 7-mile, 2,100-foot scramble starting from the first switchback on Smith Brook Road / FR 6700 and following the Lichtenwasser Lake fishing trail to a saddle on the southeast ridge. Jim Brisbine's party climbed it as a rock scramble over 20-21 September 1975, camping at Lichtenwasser Lake and continuing over the true summit to The Lichtenhorn before descending the west ridge. The winter version has you leave the road at the first major hairpin, head southwest up wooded and steep but always snowshoeable hillside, traverse toward Lichtenwasser Lake at about 4,600 ft (crossing the lake if it is frozen), then take easy slopes to the ridge crest and follow the summit ridge to the top. A winter north-side version is given with compass bearings: ski 2.6 miles up Smithbrook Road, leave it before the major switchback near 3,970 ft, follow a true bearing of 177 degrees to Lichtenwasser Lake, then 248 degrees from the lake's south end to a 5,640-foot saddle, and ascend the southeast ridge to the summit — about 5.2-plus miles, rated 2 to 2+ in skill and 2-minus in fitness, and included among the classic backcountry ski and snowboard routes in Washington. Avalanche hazard is the defining concern; both sides of the mountain present it.

before.notes: From Pelton Basin via easy slopes and a steep couloir onto the glacier (roughly 6,200-6,800 ft), then to the Magic–Pelton Col at 6,480 ft and the foot of the northeast line. Crevassed. Length apportioned within the reported 2,000 ft total.
before.pitch: Section 1 — Yawning Glacier to the base of the couloir

before.notes: Reported as sustained 40-45 degrees. This is the section most exposed to rockfall funnelled from the cliffs on either side; move through it rather than resting in it.
Reported steepening to 45-50 degrees, with 'definitely a proper 50 at the very top' and a firm crust under a few inches of soft snow in the top 100-200 ft. Pickets or a screw belay here.
Sourced: the couloir ascends via rock or snow directly to the summit, depending on the year. Watch for a cornice on the summit ridge in spring. Length apportioned to close the reported total.

before: Mesahchie Peak (8,795 ft) is the highest of four Bulger List summits on Ragged Ridge, 0.25 mi east of Katsuk Peak, between the Fisher Creek and Thunder Creek drainages in North Cascades National Park. First climbed in 1966. It's often cited as one of the hardest non-technical Bulgers on the list: the standard lines need no rope or glacier travel, but loose, blocky rock, a confusing gully/rib maze on the summit pyramid, and a long, rough cross-country traverse along the flank of Ragged Ridge from Easy Pass make route-finding and scrambling skill the real crux. Trip reports commonly note 'there's nothing easy about Easy Pass.'

before.optimalWindow: July through October, with the driest and most reliable conditions in August and early-to-mid September

July.reason: Early in the window; approach meadows are green but lingering snow from spring can still ice up the summit block

August.reason: Driest, most stable conditions ("Best window; dry rock and open trails"); also the busiest month

October.reason: Crisp, clear scrambling is still possible, but the window closes once first snows arrive; check forecasts closely late in the month

September.reason: Dry rock continues and crowds thin out after Labor Day, making it a favored month for solitude without sacrificing conditions

before: A distinct line from the standard West Route. It has been described as 'basically an alpine scramble with two pitches of harder climbing on the steepest part of the ridge,' but a recorded attempt found the ridge heavily coated in moss and heather, making the two technical pitches far slower and harder than the nominal grade suggests.

A 2012 account of down-climbing this ridge from Crowder's summit toward Pickell Pass describes it as: 'a convoluted path of grassy 3rd class ledges' with an occasional 4th class move and 'one or two short 5th class downclimbing moves... pretty tedious and definitely don't-slip-here terrain.' A several-hundred-foot-long chasm (possibly a fault) cuts across the lower ridge, and the party ultimately had to find a break in a final cliff band and a scree slope to reach Pickell Pass; one partner chose to rappel sections that the other downclimbed.

weather.typical: Wet maritime climate overall; the interior holds snow into summer, so the scramble season is a narrow dry window between snowmelt and fall storms
weather.probability: Fall storms can arrive early in the Olympics; only a 'short clear window before storms' in fall, so weather margins are tighter than typical Cascades summer objectives

before.exposure: Consequences of a slip or injury are amplified by remoteness rather than technical exposure: remote/committing terrain, lingering snow on approach slopes, and long self-evacuation distances from the deep interior near the Elwha - a straightforward Class 2-3 fall could still become a multi-day extraction

avalanche.zone: NWAC Olympics zone exists for the range, but NWAC only issues forecasts during winter storm season — N/A for this route's actual late-July-September climbing window

before.crevasses: No glacier on this line. Snow lingering on the ridge and in the gullies below it can be hard early in the season, so carry an axe until it has melted out.

before.cal: North Cascades NP backcountry permit required for Terror/Crescent basin camps; best window is late July–September once Terror Creek is fordable and the Barrier snow ramps are still consolidated.

days.note: A long, brutal bushwhack: Goodell Creek Trail to a fading climbers' path, a tricky ford of Terror Creek, then a steep, sustained climbers' trail straight up the hillside to treeline and on to a bench near The Barrier. This leg typically takes 6.5–9.5 hours depending on creek levels and route-finding.
days.title: Approach to high camp
days.objective: Reach Terror Basin / Stump Hollow high camp (~5,800–6,200 ft)

days.note: An alpine-start round trip from camp: cross The Barrier via the upper crossing just below Degenhardt into Crescent Basin, then climb a Class 4 slot to the north ridge, a Class 4-5 face to the west ridge, and an exposed Class 3 ledge to the south ridge and summit. One rappel off the summit block on the way down; loose, chossy rock throughout. Trip reports clock roughly 5.3 hours up and 3.6 hours back down.
days.title: Climb Degenhardt via the Southwest/Corkscrew Route

schedule.label: Leave high camp
schedule.detail: Alpine start with headlamps toward the upper Barrier crossing.

schedule.label: Cross The Barrier
schedule.detail: Upper crossing over moats and steep choss just below Degenhardt into Crescent Basin.

schedule.label: Start the Corkscrew line
schedule.detail: Class 4 slot gains the north ridge, then a Class 4-5 face to the west ridge.

schedule.label: Reach the summit
schedule.detail: Airy, exposed summit block; roughly 5.3 hours from camp.

schedule.label: Rappel and descend
schedule.detail: Single rappel off the summit block, then reverse the route.

schedule.label: Back at high camp
schedule.detail: Round trip from camp runs about 9 hours.

days.objective: "Summit Mount Degenhardt (8,107 ft) and return to high camp"

days.note: Reverse the Day 1 approach: down the steep hillside, re-ford Terror Creek, and follow the climbers' path and Goodell Creek Trail back to the car. Descending is a bit faster than the grind up but still a full day with the creek crossing.
days.title: Exit to trailhead
days.objective: Hike out to the Goodell Creek Cross-Country Access Trailhead

before.totalNote: A 3-day trip (commonly climbed as part of a longer Southern Pickets outing): ~18.7 miles round trip with roughly 7,500 ft of gain/loss, one long approach day, one big summit day with a rappel, and one exit day.

before.fees: $5/vehicle day-use fee or $30 annual Northwest Forest Pass required to park at the upper trailhead — pay via the on-site Scan & Pay/fee machine or display a valid Interagency/Digital Pass (cash not accepted on site). The lower trailhead is fee-free.
before.notes: No separate climbing cost-recovery fee like Mount Rainier’s $82 — the only charge is the Northwest Forest Pass (or equivalent recreation pass) for parking at the upper trailhead.
before.rules: This is a car-to-car day scramble with no camping — no NPS wilderness-permit or bear-canister rules apply here. Standard Olympic National Forest day-use etiquette (Leave No Trace, stay on the boot path) applies.
before.permit: Northwest Forest Pass (or equivalent Interagency/America the Beautiful pass) required only for upper-trailhead parking; no wilderness permit needed for day hiking.
before.closures: FS Road 2419/2419-014 is gated and snow-covered in winter and early spring; USFS lists the upper trailhead as open 'early summer through fall.' Check the Olympic National Forest alerts page for current road washouts or closures before driving up.
before.landManager: Olympic National Forest, Hood Canal Ranger District (Mount Skokomish Wilderness); district office relocated to Quilcene (295142 US-101 S, Quilcene, WA 98376), (360) 765-2200, after the former Hoodsport office closed in 2005.
before.land_manager: U.S. Forest Service — Olympic National Forest, Hood Canal Ranger District (Mount Skokomish Wilderness)
before.parking_pass: $5/vehicle day-use fee or $30 annual Northwest Forest Pass required to park at the upper trailhead — Interagency/Digital Pass also accepted (cash not accepted on site); the lower trailhead is fee-free.

overnight_permit.what: No overnight permit required on the national forest side
overnight_permit.where: Lena Lake, The Brothers camps and the Lake Cushman trailheads are in Olympic National Forest; a Northwest Forest Pass is needed to park. Camps inside Olympic National Park need a park wilderness permit.

weather.typical: Short, weather-dependent alpine window; a 'severe remote alpine environment' where storms can trap parties at camp
weather.probability: Afternoon convective buildups possible in August; early- or late-season systems bring snow and sharply raise the risk of being weathered in at a remote camp

before.exposure: Moderate to serious - Class 3-5 sections combine with steep snow/glacier where a fall could mean a crevasse fall or long slide; consequences are magnified by extreme isolation, since evacuation from this area takes days

avalanche.zone: No NWAC forecast zone specifically covers this remote glaciated summit; nearest general coverage is NWAC's North Cascades-area zones, which do not extend detailed forecasts into the summer climbing season

before.crevasses: Significant - the standard route crosses glaciated terrain and may require a bergschrund crossing; conditions shift through the season and demand roped travel and crevasse rescue readiness

before: Described in scattered sources as a 'difficult scramble via rubble' terrain; Class 3 rating implies hands-on scrambling but not roped climbing. Helmet and ice axe (early season) standard.

weather.typical: Olympic-interior maritime summer weather: generally mild and drier than winter, but the remoteness means fast-changing conditions are consequential; afternoon weather is a factor.
weather.probability: Afternoon weather is a recurring risk on the upper scramble — treat afternoon buildup/instability as a standing concern through the season.

before.exposure: 'exposure on the upper scramble' and 'loose rock and exposure' during approach/climb — a slip on the Class 3 terrain near the summit carries real fall consequence, and the remote, trail-less setting (long approach, river fords) means any injury is far from help.

avalanche.zone: NWAC 'Olympics' forecast zone exists for the range, but it is a winter/spring product and does not cover this dry, off-season (Jul-Sep) scramble route

before.crevasses: N/A - no glacier travel; the South Slopes route stays off the Queets Glacier, which sits in a cirque on the mountain's north side.

before: Steep and exposed terrain throughout - particularly dangerous during descent
Exposed down climbing through chimney sections requiring rappel stations
Active rockfall zones in off-route gullies - warning about 'moss or lichen covered rock' indicates these trap hazards
Large crevasses on Upper Curtis Glacier requiring standard glacier travel skills
Moat hazard: 'Watch out for the moat' near initial snow crossing
Upper Curtis Glacier starts to break up late season - deteriorating conditions create hazards
Late season when Winnie's Slide becomes iced: may need ice screws and second tool
Route-finding extremely difficult - 'People frequently report difficult route finding. Pay attention and don't overthink it!'
Multiple thin paths lead to cliff overlooks - serious hazard for disoriented parties
Significant weather exposure on dramatic Upper Curtis Glacier crossing
2-3 day commitment increases exposure risk

There is no maintained trail off Mount Tom's summit — climbers reverse the ascent line rather than following a distinct down-route. Downclimb the loose class 3-4 summit block and connecting ridge back to the White Glacier/Hubert Glacier saddle, then rope back up for crevassed glacier travel back across toward the Snow Dome side of the Olympus massif; at least one party climbing Olympus with a Mount Tom side objective has described this reconnection as a 'steep and loose descent off the Olympus massif' that turned back an otherwise fit, motivated group — treat it as the technical crux of the day, not an afterthought. From there, continue down over Snow Dome and re-cross the crevassed Blue Glacier to the Lateral Moraine, descend the moraine trail to Glacier Meadows camp, and reverse the Hoh River Trail (re-crossing the fixed ladder at the mile-17.5 washout) back to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb route — there is no record of fixed rappel stations or rock rappelling anywhere on Mount Tom, and the easiest route is classed simply as 'glacier + class 3 scrambling.' Glacier sections require full roped-team glacier travel gear (harness, rope, crevasse-rescue kit, pickets) rather than rappelling gear. Given the loose, exposed class 3-4 downclimbing at the Tom-Olympus connection, some parties choose to belay or hand-line short sections here even though no fixed anchors exist — carry a rope and a light rack (slings, a picket or two, maybe a picket for an improvised anchor) for that purpose, not for rappelling.
Retreat is very difficult beyond Needle Peak — the first-ascent party noted this 'would not be a good route to begin during unsettled weather'
Rock quality on the ridge crest is described in the account on record as 'wild and highly variable in quality'

Doubles 0.75"-3" (BD sizes 2-4), a single 4" (#5) piece, and singles from fingers to 1" cover the lower corner pitches; the P4 offwidth wants the #4-5 pieces though the climbing is 'surprisingly secure' via face-smears/arm-bars even where gear is sparse. Carry several extra-long slings for P2, P3, and the P5 roof traverse to control rope drag. A 60m rope is the minimum for the bolted West Face rappel descent.
Class 3-4 (reported 'reasonably solid Class 4' on the ridge, with a Class 3 option)

From a camp at Lake Doris (6,975 ft), leave the trail and head roughly northeast through open forest for about 0.6 mile, then climb the long southwest-facing talus slope, gaining about 1,400 ft to the southwest ridge/south face before finishing to the summit (8,587 ft). Terrain is Class 2 throughout: loose scree low down giving way to talus and boulders higher up. A faint climber's path along the southwest ridge is reported to be easier going than a direct line up the boulder-strewn south face. As a climb from the south the peak is described as 'a big talus bore,' while more involved, chossy climbing exists on the unfrequented east and north sides, which are not part of this standard route.

There are two real approach options for the South (Southwest) Route on Phantom Peak, and both are serious multi-day North Cascades bushwhacks — this is not a trail hike. Option one, the Luna Creek approach: from Ross Lake Resort, take the water taxi across Ross Lake (roughly $35, saves about 6 miles of paddling/road-walking) to the Big Beaver trailhead. From there it's about 9-10 miles of maintained, mostly flat, forested trail up the Big Beaver Creek drainage (through old-growth cedar groves and past beaver ponds/marshy sections) to Luna Camp, an established backcountry campsite where a NOCA wilderness permit is required. From Luna Camp the trail effectively ends; climbers leave the maintained tread and push cross-country up the Luna Creek drainage toward Phantom Peak's south side, gaining roughly 4,000+ ft over a few miles through some of the worst brush in the Cascades. Fred Beckey, on the first traverse through here in 1940, called it 'the worst imaginable struggle with flies, devil's club, willows, and alder' — modern parties confirm little has changed, reporting huckleberry, devil's club, vine maple and slide alder so dense that 0.5 mph is a good pace, plus heavy mosquito/fly pressure in summer. The creek itself must be forded in places; fords get harder (deeper, faster) the lower/farther downstream you are, so it's best to gain elevation out of the valley bottom as early as possible rather than fighting the brush along the creek itself. Water is abundant throughout (the creek and countless side-seeps), but hazard is really the terrain: no trail, no cairns, high fall-into-a-hole-in-the-brush risk, and real potential to get separated from a partner in the thick stuff (this has happened to real parties here). Above the brush line the drainage opens into subalpine meadow and talus below Phantom's south aspect. Option two, favored by several recent parties, comes from the north via Whatcom Pass: Hannegan Trailhead (3,100 ft) → Ruth Creek Trail → Chilliwack River Trail (includes a cable-car creek crossing) → Brush Creek Trail up to Whatcom Pass, then off-trail via the Whatcom Glacier and Perfect Pass to a base camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine. From that camp, the route to Phantom itself is a roughly 1,000-ft descending traverse east across snow/talus to the base of Phantom's broad southwest buttress, then up a snowfield to a saddle around 6,100 ft within the buttress — this saddle is effectively the start of the technical climbing. Whichever approach is used, expect 2-3 days of travel each way; the total round-trip distance (51.5 km / ~32 mi) reflects the Big Beaver/Luna Creek option's mileage.

before.cal: Slate Pass / Harts Pass area access road typically doesn't open until late June or July depending on snowpack, and the Pasayten is prone to wildfire smoke/closures in August-September, so early-mid July through early September is the realistic window.

days.note: From the Slate Pass / Buckskin Ridge trailhead, follow the Robinson Creek Trail down to the Middle Fork Pasayten River, then up past Freds Lake and through the Eureka Creek valley to a camp near Shellrock Pass. Mostly on trail, snow-free by midsummer, with one notable slick-log creek crossing.

before: Sentinel is most often climbed, probably almost exclusively climbed, by parties doing the famed Ptarmigan traverse. From a high camp near the LeConte–Sentinel col or on the South Cascade Glacier, parties ascend a slope to a moat on the right side of a ledge/ramp that crosses the south face; the ramp 'wasn't difficult but will keep you on your best behavior,' and the final section to the summit is straightforward Class 2-3 scrambling on snow and rock. A steeper variation exists via the west ridge, involving a steep snow ramp near 7,400 ft and a short low-5th-class rock step into a gully below the final ridge crest — this is harder than the standard line and should be treated as an alternate finish, not the default.

before.notes: Loose, poorly consolidated granodiorite rock. Described as 'one of the loosest, most unpleasant gullies.' Prone to rockfall. Width and steepness variable by season. Fast party movement essential.
Moderate snow climbing ending in easy scramble to roomy summit. May ice up overnight; better in afternoon after sun exposure. Fixed anchor present at lower ridge crux spot.

before.cal: FR-1570 (Kindy Creek Rd) has a washout, so parking is below the road-end, adding mileage; best done June-September when the Snowking Glacier has consolidated snow and the approach trail is mostly clear.

days.note: From the FR-1570 washout parking, follow the old logging road and then the boot-beaten Kindy Ridge climbers' trail up through brush and subalpine terrain, topping out around Point 5,791 before dropping to camp near Cyclone Lake. Expect a rough, steep, brushy trail with little flat ground.

After summiting, the team downclimbs to camp, breaks it down, and continues the long hike out the same day — though many parties instead camp a second night and hike out on a third day.

before.totalNote: A 2-day overnight trip is the standard: ~6.5 mi and ~4,700 ft to a Cyclone Lake camp on day 1, then a roped glacier summit push plus the full hike-out (~8.5 mi, ~2,700 ft gain / ~6,200 ft loss) on day 2; some parties split the hike-out into a third day.

before: No technical rack is needed for the standard route in normal (dry) conditions — this is an unroped class 2-4 scramble per multiple independent trip reports, including a solo ascent reported in July 2017. Parties wanting extra security for the short exposed ridge traverse near the false summit, or for a steep snow section below the saddle in early season, sometimes carry a single ~30m rope with a very light rack. A 2017 ICC group carrying 'light alpine racks, lots of doubles' up this peak explicitly reported the rack going 'mostly unused' on the South Ridge portion of their day.

Late July through September gives the most consistently snow-free, cleaned-off rock in the chute. NPS notes the trail 'can have snow or loose rock surfaces all summer,' and the chute itself can hold firm snow into early summer.

The descent does not reverse the ridge. Both of the route's rappels — about 25 m into the gap at the Pitch 7 gendarme and about 30 m off the final hoodoo tower — are made on the way up, below the last ~600 ft of scrambling to the top, so a single 60 m rope covers them. No fixed anchors are documented on this obscure, first-ascent-era route; expect natural gear anchors (horns, cracks, slung blocks) rather than bolts, and back them up — this is remote, low-traffic terrain with essentially no fixed hardware. From the summit, the descent drops onto Spectre's east-facing slopes back toward the Challenger Col/Easy Ridge approach line; in the FA party's heavy-snow-year, early-season conditions this was continuous, 'super chill' steep snow (glissade-friendly with an ice axe and the usual steep-snow/glacier caution), letting them avoid the 'typical endless scree and loose talus' that this face otherwise holds in leaner, later-season conditions — parties visiting in a low-snow year or later in the season should expect a much looser, scree/talus descent instead of snow travel. From the base, retrace the approach line back over Challenger Col, past Imperfect Impasse, along Easy Ridge, over Hannegan Pass, and out the maintained trail to the Hannegan Pass Trailhead — effectively a full reversal of the multi-day approach, not a same-day walk-off.

Described by climbers as "the classic SW ridge of the highest peak in the range": the route begins with loose, blocky climbing low down, then the final two pitches offer "wonderful easy climbing up cracks and knobs on an exposed ridge" to the summit. All routes in the Gunsight Range are short, and this one runs about 5 pitches. A 2025 trip report ("E and SW faces of Middle, S ridge of South") confirms the line is still being climbed as a distinct objective alongside the East Face. No published numeric grade was found for this route.
Pitch 6 has easy but unprotected, run-out terrain below a roof.
Pitch 7's hand traverse is exposed and "not good for a timid second."
Significant rope drag reported on some of the easier variation options.
Pitch 8's finish involves hollow, grainy flakes — test holds before committing.

weather.typical: Summer alpine weather typical of the North Cascades - generally the driest, most stable conditions of the year within the July-Sept window, consistent with the best-season/climate framing.
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms are a hazard here; the exposed granite towers and summit step raise lightning and rockfall-from-storm risk, so early starts and a weather-watch turnaround plan are warranted.

before.exposure: Consequential - loose blocks on the towers and an exposed summit step; a fall or rockfall incident on the summit block or towers would be serious given the remote, complex setting far from rescue access.

avalanche.zone: N/A - route is climbed July-Sept, outside NWAC's forecast season (NWAC issues zone forecasts roughly mid-November through mid-April only); no avalanche zone forecast applies during the climbing window

before.crevasses: Real hazard on the approach - 'crevasses and snow on the approach' across the glaciated terrain shared with the Eldorado access; roped glacier travel and crevasse-rescue readiness are required, especially earlier in the July-Sept window when snow bridges are less consolidated.

weather.typical: Dry-season alpine weather during the July–September window; afternoon thunderstorms are a recurring hazard
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms are a known hazard — plan for an early start and be off exposed talus/summit terrain by early afternoon

before.exposure: Low-technical-consequence Class 2 talus terrain, but the primary risk is the remoteness itself: "long remote northern-Pasayten approach" and "loose talus," meaning any injury or misstep translates into a serious self-rescue / evacuation problem given the distance from help

avalanche.zone: N/A - non-glaciated summer route

before: Mount Stuart (9,415 ft) is the second-highest non-volcanic peak in Washington (after Bonanza Peak) and the sixth most prominent summit in the state. It anchors the Stuart Range in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, straddling the Chelan–Kittitas county line east of Snoqualmie Pass. Its Late Cretaceous granodiorite forms one of the largest exposed granite masses in the country, with a south face that gains roughly 5,000 ft in just two horizontal miles. Fred Beckey called it "without a rival as the crown peak in the central Cascades of Washington"; the North Ridge (Grade IV, 5.9, capped by the Great Gendarme) is one of the original Fifty Classic Climbs of North America.

Avalanche Glacier is a steeper alternative to the popular South Spur route on Mount Adams. Ascends directly up a glacier with moderate ice climbing sections. More direct approach to summit than South Spur.

The published route description for this line ('South Ridge 5.4') gives the standard descent as three rappels done on a single 60m rope. One trip report on the same route mentions 'two 60-meter double rope rappels' plus a handline during their descent — read as one party choosing extra rope/redundancy for a long, loose, complex descent (8-9 linked gully/chimney/face features) rather than evidence the route requires double ropes. A single 60m (or 70m for margin) rope is standard; carrying a second, shorter rope or handline is a reasonable option for parties wanting backup on this convoluted, loose descent, not a requirement.

Anderson's Thumb has no dedicated published route description or topo. The only documented accounts are trip-report asides from parties climbing Mount Anderson: one pair was tempted to scramble it on their way out from the Anderson Glacier moraine and described it as 'a fun rock climb on good sandstone' — notably solid rock compared with the loose, meta-sedimentary terrain elsewhere on the massif — but turned back when heavy rain began. Photos from another Mount Anderson trip report show it as a recognizable landmark near the moraine/glacier basin below Echo Rock and Flypaper Pass. Treat it as an optional, unrated scramble added onto a Mount Anderson trip, not a route to travel for on its own.

weather.typical: Wet maritime west-side climate feeding a summit icecap; brief stable high-pressure windows are the norm for a summer attempt
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms/convective buildup possible in summer

before.exposure: Moderate-to-serious: crevasse fall potential on the glacier crossing plus loose rock on the final Class 2-3 summit scramble; consequences are amplified by the long, brushy, remote approach that makes self-rescue and evacuation difficult

avalanche.zone: West Slopes North Cascades; note NWAC issues formal forecasts roughly Nov-Apr, so this zone does not cover the Jul-Sep climbing season for this route

before.crevasses: Real and load-bearing hazard on the Green Lake/Diobsud Creek Glacier icecap crossing — 'glacier travel and crevasse risk'; rope up and carry crevasse rescue gear, with more open crevasses expected later in the season

before: Begins 'at the lowest part of the slab on a shallow rib' with beautiful clean, solid, grippy low-angle stone and minimal breaks. After roughly 2,000+ ft of fun, sustained 4th-class climbing the line naturally angles right and joins Timeless Treasure for brief, unexposed low-5th moves up overlaps trending up and right to the SE shoulder; easy scrambling leads to the summit block, though rock quality noticeably deteriorates on the final three pitches.

The most commonly climbed and most-described line to the summit, but every source treats it as a serious, committing objective rather than a straightforward scramble -- 'no route is easy' on Big Four. Historic trip reports document parties turning back after finding natural avalanche activity in the couloir, and describe the final downclimb as frightening even for experienced climbers.
Loose rock throughout much of the route.
Electrical storms have caught parties on this wall - the FA team described 'a terrifying electrical storm.'

Ascends the gully dividing the west face, between the main summit rock and a false summit rock to the west. Starting north of Wings, follow a narrowing gully to a large chockstone, then climb around the chockstone to the NW notch of the summit. Described as 'fun in the winter, lots of loose rock in summer.'

before.optimalWindow: Late April through June, and conditions-dependent within that window; the couloir must be filled and the snowpack consolidated

May.reason: Prime season - filled couloir with the best chance of consolidated, stable snowpack

July.reason: The couloir 'melts to loose rock and is generally out of condition' by summer - not recommended

June.reason: Still climbable most years but conditions degrade later in the month - watch for afternoon softening, increasing rockfall, and a shrinking margin before the couloir melts out

April.reason: Couloir may not yet be fully filled/consolidated this early; higher avalanche loading risk and colder, less stable snow

before: The 2003 variation's second pitch is described as 'scary, unstable class 4+ rock'
Longer and more committing than the Southwest Face — retreat is not as simple

July.reason: Scramble season opens; early-month snow patches possible on shaded slabs, improving through the month

June.reason: Snow typically still lingers on the ridge and approach ('spring: snow on the ridge; not in season'); generally too early

August.reason: Core dry-rock scramble season - most stable conditions for the slabs and approach

October.reason: Early storms and shortening days push the range out of season; not covered by the best-season window

September.reason: Still reliably dry and in-season before fall storms arrive

before: No published account gives a rappel count for this 14-pitch, 1,800 ft route — the only published descent note is "Rappel the route, which has some 60m rappels." Neither figure that circulates is supported, so none is given here. As a bound rather than a claim: station-to-station cannot exceed the pitch count, and 545 m at full 60 m rappels would be roughly 9-10.

before.notes: Granite slabs begin around 4,850 ft after the brushy lower gully. Class 2-3 scrambling on the South Buttress with slime-coated slabs near the top; Point 5872 sits on the crest here and can be bypassed on its north side. The 5,720+ ft saddle is the camp and the natural turnaround point; one party fitted two tents on a snow ledge near it.
before.pitch: 1 - Granite slabs and cliff-band navigation, ~4,850 ft to the 5,720+ ft saddle

before.grade: Class 4 bare; step-kicking snow when filled. The old standard line's notch here is reported at 65 degrees
before.notes: Beckey: 'climb 200 ft of slab to the sharp ridge leading to the summit.' This is the only section of the route where protection is a question, and no bare-rock beta has been published. In January it was good step-kicking snow. This steep notch is exactly what pushed later parties onto the southwest face.
before.pitch: 2 - 200 ft of slab above the saddle (the crux)

before.grade: Class 2-3 ridge; corniced snow crest in winter
before.notes: A rope-length or so of steep, exposed snow above the step, then an easy cruise along a broad, almost level, wide-open ridge to the 7,054 ft summit. In winter this crest is the top of the largest cornices in the area, overhanging the northeast face on the right. In summer it may instead be a scramble among rocks with steep drops on both sides.

before: Photos/comments reference "beware the belayer slayer" — suggesting rockfall exposure at belays

P1 climbs left past several bolts ('pinch the peanut and step up right into the dish'); the crux reaches right up a buttress-like feature past more bolts to chains. P2 is a shorter ~50 ft 5.10 pitch above the belay to a ledge with more chains.

before.optimalWindow: Mid-summer through early fall (roughly late July through September), once approach snow in Phelps Basin has consolidated or cleared

July.reason: Early-to-mid July can still have lingering approach snow ('snow lingers on the approach' in summer); conditions improve as the month progresses

August.reason: Best window - approach snow has generally cleared or consolidated and the scramble is at its most straightforward

September.reason: Stable early fall weather typical ('stable early, then snow returns'), but window narrows toward month's end as fall snow can return to the high basin

before.peakTraffic: A 2006 first-person account by one of the FA climbers describes the ridge as having 'remained seldom visited and rarely ascended in its entirety' six years after the 2000 FA, with only a handful of named subsequent ascents through 2005.
before.estimatePerSeason: Very low -- there are no logged ascents of this specific line, and the whole Silver Star Mountain area sees a small fraction of the traffic of Liberty Bell's Beckey Route or South Early Winters Spire's South Arête.

before: An obscure, unpolished Class 3-4 (low 5th) gully line up the east side of Esmeralda's East Peak — described by those who've climbed it as 'far from a classic,' with the crux low in the gully on wet, friable rock.

The 3 stations listed are the ridge portion only; the full descent is longer. A party on a single 60 m rope reports "a few key rappels high on the route before unroping to downclimb the remainder of the ridge... Another 7 rappels brought us down the Cat Scratch gullies to snow." Good early-season snow lets much of the couloir be downclimbed instead. The ~5-rappel / 400 ft East Ledges figure belongs to the east side descent, not this route.

before.notes: From the creek at ~2,100-2,200 ft (last certain water), 400 vertical feet of loose rock and dirt with vegetation mixed in, until the trail exits left into the trees.
Brush-free timber; a steep climber's trail goes essentially straight up for another 400 ft to the base of the slab.
Two pitches of comfortable soloing following intersecting dikes. On descent this is two double-rope rappels landing at 2,900 ft.

Continue up dirt above the upper left edge of the slab, traverse under a rock outcrop, then 40-degree loose pine-needle slopes (huckleberry stems make handholds) over the tiny notch and razorback to the Glade Saddle and its two-person bivy site. Do not drop into the dry creek bed on the west side.
A 'ramp' only relative to the cliffs around it, with a sporty 20-foot step that can be taken on either side. A single-rope rappel here on the way down.

Exposed but easier than its reputation; many parties rope up with kiwi coils. Ends at the Y Notch, the confluence of #1 and #2 Gullies at the head of the Great Canyon. Gully #1 branches right here for the Leaning Spire.
before.pitch: S6 — Key Ledge Traverse to the Y Notch

before.notes: A short exposed step around a rock band, then several hundred yards of ridiculously steep brush on a faint trail, sometimes a literal brush tunnel, to the base of #2 Gully.

Impossibly loose rock on one side, polished mossy rock on the other. Simulclimb the lower section with short belays, then pitch it out; a fixed ring piton partway up may be from the 1940 first ascent. Beckey's Chimney Variation — two leads of easy class 5 above the chimney — is preferable when the chimney is wet and rejoins at the top of the gully near 5,200 ft.

From the col at the top of #2 Gully, 'easy slabs and steep heather' to the summit — the slab is effectively unprotectable and holds the hardest move of the day for some parties. Trend to the broad final gully; the 5,519 ft summit is the tower to the west.

weather.typical: Remote glaciated alpine climate with a narrow summer window; fall turns cold and stormy, spring is snowbound, winter essentially unclimbed
weather.probability: Weather windows this deep in the range can be brief and unpredictable; afternoon buildups/thunderstorms are a possibility in summer

before.exposure: Class 4 climbing on rock noted as generally solid 'as the Pickets go' but with loose rock; combined with extreme remoteness, a fall or injury carries serious consequences given the multi-day evacuation distance

avalanche.zone: No dedicated NWAC zone covers this exact peak; nearest reference is NWAC's West Slopes North (Mount Baker) forecast, but the Pickets sit at the edge of that coverage and NWAC does not issue forecasts during the Jul-Sep climbing season — ratings below are general seasonal estimates, not NWAC-sourced

before.crevasses: Approach crosses glaciated terrain near Challenger Glacier/Luna Cirque; crevasse exposure is greatest early season and warrants roped travel

before: Frostbite Ridge is essentially a one-way, committing line — 'no turning back once you hit the ridge' — and virtually all parties descend a different, easier route rather than reversing the ridge. The standard descent is down the Sitkum Glacier: from the summit, descend the gully east of the summit into the upper Sitkum Glacier, traverse and descend to a saddle at roughly 8,000 ft, then continue down the lower Sitkum Glacier to Boulder Basin, picking up the climbers' path back to the PCT/White Chuck Trail and out to the White Chuck River Trailhead (some parties instead reverse to the Cool Glacier/Gerdine Ridge side if that's where their car is staged). The single rappel belongs to the ridge itself rather than to this walk-off descent: published route notes describe a natural belay-horn anchor (a rock horn, typically backed by old slings — inspect before trusting) just above the steep ice north of the Rabbit Ears, used to lower one pitch of steep ice into a notch referred to as the 'doorway gap' in the summit rib. This is a single-pitch rappel — a 30m single-strand rope is sufficient for the drop described — encountered while working through the crux ice/rock step near the Rabbit Ears (i.e., on the way up for most parties, since the standard descent avoids the ridge entirely); some parties simul-climb this step with screw/picket protection instead of rappelling, depending on ice conditions. Carry 3–4 ice screws and/or pickets for this section and for the steep snow/ice above the Rabbit Ears regardless of whether you end up rappelling it.
Description flags hold quality uncertainty ("holds should hold") — test holds before committing
A single 60m rope works for the descent with careful planning; double ropes give more flexibility
Highly rated, and called 'the best climb I've ever done in the North Cascades' by one of its first ascensionists

Confirmed as Mount Index's Main Peak, Hourglass Gully (Winter), Grade III/1,900 ft. Class 4/low 5th rock plus a short section of 60+ degree snow/ice/tree climbing on the East Ridge, which is often rappelled on descent. Protection note: 'pickets, slings for trees' — snow pickets and tree slings are the primary protection, not a rock rack. Ice tools/crampons required.

A 75-ft/23m rope is enough for the short belays/lowers on the Northwest Ridge, but rappelling the 100-ft summit gully in one go takes a 60m rope doubled — with the short rope, plan to downclimb the gully
Bring pickets specifically for the Ruth and Icy Glacier crossings, not just the ridge
Go early-to-mid summer, before the glaciers reported 'down to bare ice' in some years

Source material describes this as 'variable; several rappels (2-3+) commonly used descending the upper ridge/east face, backed up where anchors are marginal' without exact locations, lengths, or anchor specifics per rappel. Web research to firm this up was inconclusive (search budget exhausted, no usable trip-report results returned).
