weather.typical: Heavy North Cascades maritime snowpack with glaciers/lingering snow into summer
weather.probability: Early fall storms can arrive by September; summer afternoon thunderstorms are possible in the North Cascades though not specifically documented for this peak

before.exposure: Class 2-3 scrambling near the summits with loose rock; the greater consequence driver is the sheer remoteness and length of the approach — a slip, injury, or weather change far from any road access is a serious self-rescue problem in extreme remoteness

avalanche.zone: Approximate NWAC 'West Slopes North' zone (covers the North Cascades/Glacier Peak Wilderness area), but NWAC does not issue forecasts during the July-September climbing season, so no route-specific in-season avalanche rating exists

before.crevasses: Real hazard on the Suiattle/White Chuck Glacier crossing en route to the peaks; more concealed and dangerous early season when snow bridges are intact, more visible and avoidable by late summer/early fall as about 'snowfields and possible glacier travel on the Glacier Peak massif flanks'

May.reason: General Liberty Bell rock "comes into condition" starting in May per regional guidance, but Washington Pass Hwy access and route-specific conditions can still be unsettled

June.reason: Rock typically in condition once the highway is fully open

September.reason: Rock remains climbable "until the autumn storms," which regionally tend to arrive in October

before: Grade: 5.12 (YDS), Grade IV overall. 11 pitches, approximately 1,100 feet of climbing. Route follows intricate crack systems and faces on East Face of Liberty Bell. Hazards: significant rock fall danger in approach gully (described as "party-induced rock fall bowling alley"); loose rock throughout approach; exposed alpine terrain; weather exposure on big wall. Required skills: advanced alpine rock climbing, 5.11+ crack climbing, self-rescue, anchor building, multi-pitch experience. First ascent: 1967 (aid climbing); free ascent variation established 2008 by Mikey Schaefer. Best season: June-September; July-September strongly preferred (late June requires ice axe, crampons). Notable: route features substantial fixed gear on most pitches; descent via two-rope rappel from M&M Ledge or summit traverse.

before.fall: Cool and often clear, with larch color in nearby basins by late September, but increasing chance of early-season snow.
before.spring: Snowbound through at least June at these elevations; access road/trails typically not clear until late June.
before.summer: Warm to hot days with cool nights; afternoon thunderstorms are common in the high country.
before.winter: Heavy snow and cold; the peak and access roads are effectively inaccessible.
before.typical: Dry, sunnier east-slope-Cascades climate compared to the west side, but still exposed and cold at elevation — expect cold nights and possible summer thunderstorms even in August. Snow can linger on north aspects and passes into early-mid July.

bySeason.fall: Larches turn gold in Eureka Creek/Shellrock Basin in late September, but a documented late-Sept trip found the high ridges already "snowy, cold, and wind-blasted" — treat late season as shoulder winter conditions.
bySeason.spring: Passes and approach trails are typically snow-covered and not practical for this route.
bySeason.summer: Late July through September is the reliable snow-free window for the high passes (Rolo, Shellrock, Butte); a normal winter clears most routes by early-mid July.
bySeason.winter: Not a winter objective — Harts Pass Road and interior trails are snowbound and the wilderness is essentially inaccessible.

before.forecastZone: NWS Zone WAZ049 (Western Okanogan County), which covers the Mazama/Winthrop/Twisp/Pasayten area

before.optimalWindow: Mid-July through September; late July-August is the core dry window

July.reason: Early July can still carry lingering snow patches; conditions generally firm up toward mid-month, matching the 'mid-July through September' best-season start

June.reason: Spring conditions are snowbound with avalanche terrain; gullies and slabs on this route are likely still snow-filled

August.reason: Core dry season per existing climate.typical ('prime season, mostly dry with snow patches early'); most stable rock and driest approach conditions

September.reason: Still within the best-season window, but with cooler temps, shorter days, and possible early storms late in the month

before: Mount Crowder has no trailhead and no maintained trail — every ascent is layered onto a multi-day, off-trail traverse through the heart of the Picket Range, and Crowder is almost never climbed as a standalone objective. Parties reach it via one of two corridors. From the south: the Goodell Creek climbers' path (turn off WA-20 opposite Newhalem into Goodell Creek Campground; the boot path starts behind a large boulder at the campground) climbs steeply and brushily through slide alder and old-growth timber, gaining roughly 2,500 ft in about a mile to reach the basins below McMillan Spire/Inspiration Peak in the Southern Pickets; from there it's a rugged, unmarked cross-country traverse north over intervening cols (Crescent Creek Basin, the shoulder east of Mount Terror, and bypasses around the McMillan Cirque "Barrier") toward the range's central saddle area. From the north/east: the Big Beaver Trail out of the Ross Dam trailhead on Ross Lake (often shortened with the Ross Lake Resort water taxi to Big Beaver/Beaver Pass Camp), leaving trail to climb Access Creek — staying on its north-flank benches through semi-open forest to about 3,700 ft, where brush thickens and a faint, cairned climbers' path crosses to the south bank and continues to the open basin at the creek's headwaters (reliable water, good camping). From either entry, Crowder itself is gained by traversing the connecting ridge past Pioneer Peak and Phantom Peak to Wild Pass, a heather-and-talus notch overlooking the small tarn of Wild Lake just below; from the pass, cross open slopes to the col between Phantom Peak and Crowder, then climb the broad SW Flank — tersely put, "climb SW from the col" — up easy 2nd/3rd-class scree, heather ramps, and low-angle rock to the summit. There is no reliable water above Wild Lake, and the connecting terrain between passes is exposed talus and heather with genuine routefinding difficulty in poor visibility; expect several full days of off-trail travel carrying multi-day loads to even reach Wild Pass.

This is rated 3rd class with only minor snow/ice difficulty; the glacier 'has experienced significant recession in recent years' but remains 'very reasonable' with good navigation and some scrambling. Early season, access the glacier via a snow finger on climber's right; late season, bypass via Class 3 scrambling left of the glacier. Cross the moat, ascend the upper glacier toward Mount Daniel's West Pyramid, and reach the col between the Middle and True summits.

The route climbs the northeast buttress of Mt. Despair's north summit, starting low in the green, rugged Goodell Creek valley. It opens with roughly 1,300 ft of 5.6 climbing up an open-book corner on the lower buttress, followed by scenic but progressively technical scrambling over a series of notches that require short rappels to pass. The crux is a deep cleft (several hundred feet) near the top of the upper buttress; the first-ascent party found a 70m, 5.9 pitch up a right-trending ramp through it after judging the opposite wall too steep, loose, and hard to access. A shorter technical pitch and more moderate climbing follow, then a final 70m steep rock pitch gains the upper north ridge, which is followed via a snow ridge to the summit. The first ascensionists described it as technically rewarding but requiring serious effort just to reach — 'like eating a gourmet meal off a dirty floor.'

July.reason: Early July can still carry heavy lingering snowpack ('heavy lingering snow; avalanche hazard' in spring bleeding into early summer); conditions generally improve and firm up by mid-to-late July

August.reason: The best window - snow has cleared from most of the route and the long approach is most reliable

September.reason: Still climbable in early September, but with shortening days and early storm possibility, which is a real concern this far from an escape route

before: West Peak carries the official USGS 'Mount Fury' benchmark and, via its long, loose connecting ridge from East Fury, is markedly harder than its twin summit — West Fury is routinely listed among the '10 hardest peaks in Washington by their easiest route.' Precise modern surveying has found that East Fury is actually roughly 20 ft taller than West Fury (about 8,322 ft vs. roughly 8,300 ft), meaning the officially named summit is not the range's true high point, even though it remains the far more serious technical objective. The standard route climbs East Fury first, then follows a wild, exposed ridge traverse over three loose towers/gendarmes to reach West Fury's summit — typically adding a full 12-16+ hour day, with a real chance of a forced bivouac, onto an already multi-day Northern Pickets expedition.

No reliable cell service beyond about a mile past the Hoh Rain Forest Visitor Center; the Blue Glacier basin is effectively a dead zone. Park guidance is not to rely on a phone to "bail you out" — carry a satellite communicator or PLB.

From Crescent Creek Basin, ascend broad granite slabs up toward the saddle between Mount Terror and Mount Degenhardt, then follow the short, steep summit ridge directly to the top — described as offering 'challenges beyond that of a normal alpine rock climb' despite its modest 5.6 rating, due to looseness and exposure on the upper ridge.

fitnessSpec.hiking: Strong multi-day backpacking fitness - the approach via Royal Basin/Dungeness-area trails to the high camp below The Needles is long and largely off-trail near the top, typically making this a 2-3 day car-to-car trip rather than a dayhike-able objective.
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Overnight/multi-day pack weight (camp gear + several days food) for the approach, dropped to a light scrambling kit for the actual summit push through the loose Class 3-4 terrain.

before.approachTime: Full day (or more) approach-hike to a high camp near The Needles, followed by a separate scramble summit day - realistically a 2-3 day round trip, not a single-push dayhike for most parties.
requiredSkills: off-trail route-finding and navigation (map/compass or GPS) in the Olympic backcountry
rockfall awareness and party spacing on loose terrain
basic glacier/snow travel or steep-snow competence for early-season attempts when snowfields linger on the approach
self-arrest / careful footing on loose talus and choss
before.experienceLevel: Solid Class 3-4 scrambling experience is mandatory, ideally with prior exposure to loose/rotten alpine rock ('notoriously loose rock in The Needles', 'exposed spire scrambling'). This is not a beginner scramble - partners should have done comparable off-trail Class 3-4 Olympics or Cascades objectives before, and be comfortable route-finding without a marked path.

before: A 5-pitch, mostly-independent 5.9 line up low-angle ramps and corners on the same wall as Wright-Pond, joining that route's final two pitches to reach the top; recorded as a "partial new route" since its upper section repeats existing climbing.

before.grade: Moderate snow slope, can firm to hard ice
before.notes: Broad, moderately angled couloir on the NW side of the peak; described as wide and "not terribly steep" when soft, but reported "shockingly icy and smooth" requiring careful crampon work in a May 2024 ascent.
Above the head of the couloir, roughly 800 vertical feet of loose, dry talus-hopping on the north ridge leads to the summit.

before: Four single-rope rappels (60 m) from the East Ridge notch down to the Argonaut-Colchuck col, and this is a traverse descent off the east side - not a reversal of the arete. Two independent published descriptions give the same sequence, and a 2022 party counted 'the 1st of 4 rappels'. Three is also correct for a party that downclimbs the short loose gully at station 2 instead of rappelling it; the difference is that one optional rappel, not a rope-configuration difference.

Previous parties had reportedly been turned back below this ridge by the area's fickle weather, or reconsidered after sizing up the base — the climbing itself is 'engaging but surprisingly moderate' (mostly 5.7+) once committed
Carry a spare nut/sling for tensioning across the pitch-6 gap in case the 5.10 stem doesn't go clean
The "Bela Lugosi Traverse" below the summit dihedral is exposed and unnerving even though it's only moderate in technical difficulty.
The descent ridge traverse to the Blob/Terror col is described by the first ascensionists as "an adventure in itself," requiring short simul-climbing over exposed terrain.
The Barrier crossing on approach is loose, dirty class 3 terrain — a slip here would be serious.

The South Ridge / McAllister Glacier route approaches Primus from the opposite (Cascade River Road/Eldorado) side of the mountain rather than via Thunder Creek, crossing the Eldorado, Inspiration, and North Klawatti/McAllister Glaciers through the Klawatti–Austera high country. It's commonly climbed as part of the Inspiration Traverse or combined with Austera, Klawatti, and/or Tricouni Peaks rather than as a standalone objective — one climber who did it called Primus 'one of the most remote' of Washington's Bulger List summits.
The thin traversing first pitch has real fall consequences onto a ledge below — described locally as "don't fall or your shins are toast."

Corrected from 2, which covered only the ridge above the notch and omitted the couloir. A published route description gives about five rappels, descending by rappelling and downclimbing the route. A two-rope party logged three — 20 m into the gully, 10 m to the belay anchor, then "a final 30-meter rappel delivered us to the Quien Sabe Glacier", using both ropes for the last. Anchors along this line are documented as blocky and inconsistent — inspect before trusting.

before.peakTraffic: Described as 'probably the second most popular route in the Liberty Bell Group' after the Beckey Route on Liberty Bell; guides advise an early start and weekday timing to avoid crowds
before.estimatePerSeason: High — by far the most trafficked SEWS technical route

before.fitnessSpec: Trailhead to the Sulphide Glacier camp ~4-6 hrs; summit day from camp ~8-10 hrs round trip
before.approachTime: Trailhead to the Sulphide Glacier camp about 4-6 hrs; summit day from camp roughly 8-10 hrs round trip
requiredSkills: Class 3-4 scrambling with some low-5th-class moves (about 5.3, or 5.6-5.7 held strictly to the crest)
Rappelling with a 60m rope for descent
before.experienceLevel: Intermediate alpine climber — accessible to parties with solid glacier-travel basics; a common 'first big glaciated alpine objective' route

before: Rappel the ridge from any station; fixed anchors ('typical Cascades rap tat') have been reported at multiple points.
Striking pitch-3 liebeck crack, Great Gendarme offwidth crux, 5.5 slab with a good crack up top. Rock 'loose in spots, lichen covered' in places.

The Tempest was originally aided by its first ascensionists and later freed ground-to-summit; most parties who top out on the summit ridge use the standard Colchuck Balanced Rock walk-off: class 3-4 scrambling around the right (south) side of the true summit block to a broad sandy/scree gully, with a short step near the top sometimes eased by a single ~30m (100ft) rappel to the east off a sling around a horn (natural anchor, not bolted) — many parties simply downclimb this step instead. From there it's a loose scree/talus descent, clockwise around the peak, back to the base of the route (45 min-1hr). Parties who don't want the loose summit scramble — or who are bailing partway — instead rappel the route itself, tree-to-tree on natural anchors; one trip account notes it 'can be rappelled with two 60m ropes' to avoid the loose walk-off. Over the route's ~9 pitches (roughly 1,000+ ft) that works out to somewhere around 7-9 tree-anchor rappels with double 60m ropes. Watch for rope-snag risk in trees and loose blocks on this alpine wall either way.

Pitch 1 (5.10-, 6 bolts + gear to a chain anchor): a thin corner crack (~5.8) on small cams leads to low-fifth climbing before the first bolt at ~35 ft, then mixed bolts/gear to a large ledge, then short 5.10 climbing to anchors. Pitch 2 (5.10, 7 bolts to a 2-bolt anchor): bolts traverse right; well-bolted and takes no gear, but 'a bit chossy and dirty' as of 2025, with one bolt hidden until higher and the climber going out of the belayer's sight.

before.name: Snow Lake Trail to Great Scott Bowl and Pineapple Pass
before.notes: Upper Alpental lot at the end of Alpental Road (about 3,100 ft), I-90 exit 52. Take the Snow Lake Trail (#1013) north; a cat track runs up the valley from the end of the lot, just left of the stream, before the tread narrows to normal trail. At roughly 1.5-1.6 miles a small signed junction splits Source Lake from Snow Lake — bear left toward Source Lake. Cross the Source Lake basin contouring near 4,000 ft, then at about 4,400 ft you crest a lip and drop into Great Scott Bowl (also called Pineapple Basin). Work up the bowl on talus, or on snow if any remains, toward Pineapple Pass at the head of it, passing beneath the Fang — the pinnacle on the bowl's west side that carries the Edge of Time route. The common error is here, not lower down: a boot path running around the back of the Fang leads into the gully between the Fang and the Tooth. Parties who take it have to backtrack several hundred feet through trees and rock fields to get back onto the right ground. The second error is going straight up to Pineapple Pass itself — that col is the rappel line down, not the way up.
hazards: loose talus underfoot the whole length of Great Scott Bowl
steep sustained snow slope below Pineapple Pass in early season - axe, sometimes crampons
moat, and in some years a cornice, where the bowl's snow meets rock at the pass
rockfall from parties above on a face that is often busy
no reliable water past the Source Lake outlet
before.baseFinding:
From Great Scott Bowl, scramble to the notch just south of Pineapple Pass, then contour clockwise around the Tooth's south side. The last part of that contour is short class 3-4 and is not exposed; if it feels serious you are on the wrong ground.

You are at the start when you are standing under a broad, blocky face roughly 400 ft high with an obvious big vertical crack system splitting it. The first moves are easy ramps that angle left to a large rectangular block, then back right into that crack system. About 100 ft up, the first belay is a slung rock horn with a balanced, flat-topped block sitting on it — that block is the confirmation you are on the standard line.

Two negative markers. If you are looking up a steep, narrow gully rather than an open face, you are in the gully between the Fang and the Tooth, one formation short — go back down and continue around. And if you scrambled straight up into a notch with rappel slings hanging above you, you are standing at Pineapple Pass on the descent route; downclimb and take the next notch south, then contour.

In early season a steeper gully runs up toward the base of the face. Do not use it unless it is filled with snow.

before.name: Winter and spring, snow-covered Alpental valley
before.notes: Once there is meaningful snow the summer tread is not the route. The talus slopes the summer trail crosses are the Alpental valley's avalanche chutes — seventeen of them are counted along its length — and the winter line instead climbs the valley on the south side of the South Fork Snoqualmie toward Source Lake rather than following the summer switchbacks across those paths. From below Source Lake, traverse up into Great Scott Bowl, typically on an upward-traversing line on the west side of the bowl passing beneath the Fang, and join whatever track leads to Pineapple Pass. Most parties cache skis or snowshoes in the bowl before the final slope. The entire trip through the Source Lake and Snow Lake basins is avalanche terrain; this is a stability decision, not a route-finding one.
hazards: avalanche terrain the full length of the Alpental valley - roughly seventeen chutes cross the summer trail line
the summer boot path is not a safe winter line once snow is present
cornices at Pineapple Pass
moat between the snow and the rock at the top of the bowl
creek crossings near the Source Lake outlet at high early-season flow
before.baseFinding:
The finish is the same: the notch just south of Pineapple Pass, then a clockwise contour. Under snow the thing that decides where you can actually reach rock is the moat at the top of the bowl's snow. Probe it, and be ready to work around its edge on rock rather than force the direct step across.

With the base buried, the 'easy ramps left to a large rectangular block' start can be under snow. If you cannot find that block, you are probably below the true start — keep contouring around rather than climbing the first weakness above you, which is what puts parties into the gully between the Fang and the Tooth.

before: Approached from a multi-day camp in Crescent Creek Basin (reached via the Goodell Creek / Terror Creek / Barrier approach), the route crosses roughly a mile of basin terrain before climbing a chockstone-filled gully system rated up to 5.7 (logged elsewhere as 'S. Face - West Twin Needle, II-5th class'). Loose rock and route-finding are the main challenges; parties commonly climb this as a side objective from a Southern Pickets base camp rather than a stand-alone trailhead-to-summit day.

Mount Torment (8,120+ ft) is a granite peak on the west wall of Boston Basin in the North Cascades, Skagit County. It was first climbed August 23, 1946 by Jack Schwabland and Herb Staley, who named it for 'the torture of a hot day with only one orange for quenching thirst.' The peak is best known today as the western anchor of the Torment-Forbidden Traverse, a mile-long connecting ridge to neighboring Forbidden Peak (8,815 ft) that is one of the most sought-after moderate alpine outings in the Cascades and is closely linked to Forbidden's West Ridge, a route in Roper & Steck's Fifty Classic Climbs of North America.

No roped rock rack is carried on this route. Cross-referenced trip reports consistently describe the non-standard North Ridge (via the Wolf Creek/Gardner Meadows trail and an old, largely-vanished mine boot path) as an unroped Class 2-3 scramble: talus and scree to Gardner Meadows, then an unmaintained path/cairns to a tarn and a spur ridge onto the crest, then a 'pick-your-own-adventure' scramble along the ridge crest with 'a few class 3 moves' on a spur ridge. No party describes placing cams, nuts, or using a rope.

No published trip-report rack list was found. The first-ascent note (Scott Bennett & Blake Herrington, 2012) describes ~160m of climbing as 'an incredible fingers-to-thin-hands splitter, then a series of left-leaning roofs, surmounted by hand cracks and jugs.' Based on that description, expect doubles in the finger-to-hand range (roughly 0.3-1) for the splitter, plus singles up to #3 for the hand cracks, and a full nut set for the thin sections.

Descend Anderson's Thumb by reversing the ascent line: a single rappel from the summit block back down to the notch/col it rises from. The pinnacle is short (climbers describe it as "a fun rock climb on good sandstone," essentially a one-pitch spire), so a single-strand rappel on a 30m rope or a doubled 60m rope is enough to reach the col; because this is an obscure, lightly-visited objective with no documented fixed hardware, expect a natural anchor — a sling around a horn, block, or chockstone — rather than bolts or chains, so carry cordage/rap rings and be prepared to leave gear or build your own anchor. From the col, downclimb/scramble back to Flypaper Pass and recross the upper Eel Glacier (rope up for crevasse hazard — parties have noted a bergschrund cutting across this descent line in recent seasons), then reverse the snow/scree slope down to the Anderson Glacier moraine camp. From there it's a full reversal of the approach: drop to Anderson Pass, follow the West Fork Dosewallips Trail back through Honeymoon Meadows to the Dosewallips Ranger Station, then the road-walk/bike-out. Given the ~38-mile round-trip distance and remote setting, most parties treat this as a multi-day trip and descend only to high camp the day of the climb, hiking out the following day rather than going car-to-car.
The final summit move is on an unprotectable friction slab — a fall here would be serious.
The upper-mountain scree is unusually loose ('kitty litter over sand'), even by North Cascades standards.
There are no reliable water sources once you leave Willow Creek.

Described generically as 'Class 3, exposed scrambling — gear and experience recommended.' Route-specific South Ridge trip reports were sparse; inferred that a rope is not typically carried for the ridge scramble itself given comparable Class 3 Cascades scrambles, though some parties may carry a short rope/sling for exposed moves.

This is one of the two main routes on Cannon Mountain and is 'only advised as an ascent route' -- most parties descend via the standard Prusik Pass/Druid Plateau line instead of reversing it. It's best done in mid-to-late summer once snow has melted from around Coney Lake and off the ridge. The route starts at the Stuart Lake Trailhead, climbs steep, bushy, loose burned slopes to the ridge crest, then follows and traverses below the crest -- including a notorious 0.3-mile loose traverse below a band of towers that can't be climbed directly -- before a talus gully and short final scramble to the summit block.

Documented only informally — no page with pitch-by-pitch beta was found. The line begins on Chair's north ridge and follows the crest toward Bryant on 4th-class to low-5th-class rock, with one short, steep mandatory rappel (~50 ft) getting off Bryant — the same rappel found on the closely related 'Tooth - Chair Traverse,' which covers the Bryant-to-Chair portion of this ridge system.

"Some 5.6 climbing on solid rock that rejoins the East Face route about halfway up." Instead of the standard route's loose rock, this variation deals with a moat, which parties cross by building a snow anchor with a picket and jumping the gap. 7 pitches, 1,120 ft total.

Start at the White River Trailhead (~2,300 ft, end of White River Road/FR-6400). Follow White River Trail #1507 south along the flat valley floor for about 4 miles - easy grade but notoriously buggy/mosquito-heavy in early-to-mid summer - to its junction with Boulder Creek Trail #1562. Turn onto Boulder Creek Trail and climb roughly 4.5 miles through forest into Boulder Creek Basin, fording Boulder Creek (unbridged) around 4,000 ft; in early season this crossing is cold and knee-to-thigh deep and sometimes braids into two or three separate channels. Established camps sit in the open basin between about 4,900 and 5,300 ft (roughly 8.5 miles and ~3,000 ft of gain from the car), and given the scale of this outing (~22-23 miles round trip, 6,200-6,500+ ft one-way gain to the summit) most parties treat this as a base camp rather than a car-to-car day. From camp, leave the maintained trail and climb open heather/talus north toward Boulder Pass (~6,300 ft) - a direct fall-line push from about 5,800 ft takes roughly 1.5 hours. Two lines diverge from the pass area: for the glacier line, go down steep snow on the far side of the pass and climb to a bench near 6,700 ft on Clark's eastern arm, and rope up there for crevassed glacier travel (crampons and axe required); then traverse east across the basin under Peak 7242, crossing its NE ridge near 6,700 ft, then turn west (~30 min) to reach the toe of the Walrus Glacier (marked 'Clark Glacier' on some maps). For the non-glacier south-basin alternative, stay climber's-left, gain the south ridge of Pt. 8373 on open heather, and locate what published notes call 'the one and only easy gully' near 7,200-7,300 ft breaching the summit rock band; contour broken rock and lingering snow to the final south/west ridge and a short class 3 scramble to the summit. Water is reliable along the White River and in Boulder Creek Basin but essentially absent above camp - fill up before the push. Key hazards: the unbridged Boulder Creek ford, heavy mosquitoes on the valley approach, wet-slide/avalanche-prone slopes on the basin traverse into early summer, and genuine route-finding difficulty picking the correct gully/ridge above the basin - parties have gotten cliffed out searching for it.

weather.typical: Westside North Cascades maritime climate - heavy snowpack feeds the Colonial Glacier, keeping the mountain snow-covered outside the mid-summer window.
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms are common in the North Cascades in July-August; plan for an early alpine start (pre-dawn) to be off exposed terrain before they build.

before.exposure: Consequential terrain in two zones: sustained steep snow with long runout below/on the glacier approach and exposed Class 3-4 summit rock scrambling near the top; a fall in either is high-consequence given the remote, glaciated, off-trail setting.

avalanche.zone: Approximately NWAC "West Slopes North" zone (west side of the Cascade crest along the SR 20 corridor) - no NWAC zone is drawn specifically around Colonial Peak, and NWAC's daily forecast season (roughly Nov-May) does not cover this route's Jul-Sep climbing window

before.crevasses: Primary technical hazard ("crevasse fall on the Colonial Glacier"): snow bridges are most reliable early-mid summer and progressively weaken/open through August-September as the glacier melts out.

before: First climbed the same day as the peak's other documented technical line (July 31, 1963), by a separate Mountaineers rope of four who 'climbed directly up the east face from the glacier (class 3-4),' during that season's Northern Pickets climbs. No later account describing a repeat of this specific line was found; modern parties have used the northwest-couloir/north-ridge line instead.

Dark Side of Liberty climbs the northeast face of Liberty Bell and is noted by its first-ascent party as being 'about 20 minutes from the road' — the shortest approach of the major Liberty Bell technical lines. Park at the hairpin turn on WA-20 east of Washington Pass (same general area as the East Face approach) and follow the cairned path from the pond toward the East Face, then contour toward the northeast aspect of the wall rather than continuing all the way into the main East Face talus. Given the short, steep nature of this approach, expect some scrambling/scree underfoot near the base; carry a helmet through any loose sections.
Go in late spring. Snow suppresses the brush, snowmelt supplies the water this slope does not have, and the avalanche hazard on the south side is minimal.

Study the map before you leave the car. Every account stresses route-finding through the rock outcrops; one party made it up without backtracking through a combination of careful map study and, in their own words, blind luck.
Beckey's line above the 5,720+ ft saddle is '200 ft of slab to the sharp ridge leading to the summit'. In good snow that is step-kicking. Bare, it is class 4 and worth a rope.
The 65-degree notch on the ridge is the reason the southwest face variation exists. If steep snow is not your thing, take the SW face instead.
Take the south ridge crest on descent, not the east-basin variation. The step into the saddle looks worse than it is and has all the ledges you need.
The summit crest is the top of very large cornices overhanging the northeast face — the biggest wall in the state. Walk well back from the edge, especially in flat light.
Do not confuse this with the Davis Peak near Cle Elum, which has a maintained trail. This one does not, and never has.

before.notes: Climbs left past bolts ('pinch the peanut, step up right into the dish'); crux reaches right up a buttress feature past bolts to chains.
~50 ft second pitch above the belay to a ledge with more chains.

before.name: Eldorado Creek Trailhead (Cascade River Road)
before.note: Same Cascade River Road trailhead as the standard route; Timberline Mountain Guides' route description explicitly starts 'the standard climber's trail from the North Fork Cascade River up Eldorado Creek and into the basin of Roush Creek' before diverging west toward the Eldorado/Triad notch and West Face.

before: Navigation complexity exceeds the technical difficulty — 'Garfield is a hazardous enigma'
Occasional thick vegetation along the ledge traverses
5th class, easy to moderate (FA account: 'easy to moderate fifth-class pitches')

Extremely committing - very long approach with lots of up and down: difficult to retreat once committed
Total mileage 40+ miles (up Frostbite, down Cool Glacier) - multi-day commitment increases exposure
Most parties take 2-3 days - extended alpine exposure risk
Seasonal variation: 'Route may be snow in early season, expect more ice later in year'
Snow slopes up to approximately 45 degrees with steep angle exposure

Alpine ice face requiring 1-2 pitches of technical climbing

Best in a narrow spring window when the couloir holds consolidated snow; one trip report specifically notes the route 'usually has a small window in the spring.' A winter ascent has also been documented, and an early-summer (late June) ascent was reported, but conditions are more variable outside spring.

The route begins in a shallow, down-sloping depression with awkward climbing off two fixed pins, then follows the crest as directly as possible over several rock steps and across two significant notches to the summit, with the crux (5.9) typically encountered higher on the route. American Alpine Institute reports 'the climbing quality is lower than that of the Blue Buttress' and that 'protection is a bit hard to find in spots.' It is also notably longer than its neighbor — subsequent parties have reported as many as 12-17 roped pitches, and one climber compared its character to the South Arete of South Early Winters Spire, 'except that it was over a thousand feet long.'

The lower northeast ridge section climbs 4th-to-easy-fifth-class (5.4 max) slabs and cracks on excellent rock. It's followed by the crux upper east-face pitch, graded 5.6 X on rock described as horrible, with almost no protection - this 'is not a good route for the average 5.6 climber' and choosing the wrong line on the face 'could have fatal consequences.' A 70 m rope and a light alpine rack are needed.

With a reported 6+ hour round-trip time and full sun exposure that makes the route 'hot in the summertime,' start early enough to be well clear of the technical pitches before peak afternoon heat, and set a firm car-to-car turnaround based on your party's pace on similar 8-pitch routes.

Reaching Luna Cirque is the crux of the trip. The historical approach follows the Big Beaver Trail from Ross Lake (a $35 water taxi from Ross Lake Resort cuts about 6 miles off the hike) up to Luna Camp, then climbs steeply beside Luna Creek into the cirque — Fred Beckey himself described this bushwhack as 'the worst imaginable struggle with flies, devil's club, willows, and alder.' Most contemporary parties instead approach via Access Creek, which branches off that same Big Beaver Trail rather than a separate trailhead — parties continue on the maintained trail roughly a mile past Luna Camp to the unmarked Access Creek/Big Beaver Creek confluence, then leave the trail there to follow the Access Creek drainage (with an occasional bootpath) up into the cirque — a longer but far less brutal line than Luna Creek.

before.notes: Cross the moat via a chockstone-filled gully, then climb several sustained, difficult pitches on compact granite to gain the ridge crest (first ascent line; a 2020 repeat logged at least 3 pitches, hardest 5.9).

before: Royal Basin approach crosses the top edge of a small glacier where crevasse danger is described as minimal; remainder is Class 2 loose scree/pillow lava. Described as 'steep, exposed and quite serious' primarily due to rockfall risk, not technical difficulty — helmet essential, rope not standard.

Approach is up a brush-choked valley low in the Goodell Creek drainage — described by the first-ascent party as rough enough that 'seasoned Cascades aficionados balked' at it. This is the opposite (northeast) side of the peak from the standard Triumph Pass/Despair Lakes approach.

Descend the same line used on ascent — Fernow's summit sits atop a maze of loose gullies and there is no reliable shortcut. From the top, downclimb the class 4 (occasionally low 5th, but the harder moves can be sidestepped) summit block; some parties, especially in wet rock or with a less experienced group, sling a horn or block on the north side of the block for a quick single rappel instead of downclimbing the crux moves — there are no fixed or bolted anchors on this route, so bring a couple of slings/rap rings to build a natural anchor, and a 30 m rope is sufficient (it's used to protect just the short crux section, not to reach the ground, so most parties still downclimb the remainder). Below the block, retrace the choss gully to about 8,800 ft, re-cross the exposed sloped-slab traverse with care (more consequential descending than ascending), then continue down the talus/scree valley back toward the glacier remnant, watching again for the crevasse near the plateau. From there you must reclimb roughly 1,000 ft back up to the Seven Fingered Jack col before dropping into Leroy Basin; an alternate some parties use off the col instead drops climber's-right across sandy ledges and down through large boulders directly to the basin, trading the reclimb for its own loose, ankle-twisting terrain. Trip reports consistently describe the descent as worse underfoot than the climb up — expect a 'huge amount of loose rock,' near-misses, and slips — so wear a helmet the whole way and plan to be off the summit block and crux traverse before dark. From Leroy Basin, reverse the steep climbers' trail back down to Phelps Creek Trail #1511 and out to the trailhead. Because the round trip from Leroy Basin alone can run 10-13+ hours, most parties treat the climb as a 2-3 day trip, camping at Leroy Basin going in and out rather than pushing car-to-car in a day.

before: Descend the same north-ridge line used on ascent: from the summit, reverse the class 3 gully above the notch (some parties find an alternate exposed gully slightly east of the ascent line 'looks manageable from above' but funnels into the same terrain) and downclimb to the crux 7,300-7,400 ft notch. This notch is the one place on the route where parties differ — many downclimb it unroped on adequate but exposed hand/footholds, while others back off with a single rappel of roughly 30 m/100 ft. There is no fixed or bolted rappel station here: any anchor is a natural one (slung block, horn, or krummholz/tree) built by the descending party, and old rappel webbing/cord has been reported at the notch by multiple parties of unclear age and origin — treat any found tat as unverified and back it up or replace it rather than trusting it outright. Below the notch, work back down through the talus and snow, staying on the west side of the cliff bands to avoid the steeper, more exposed rock, then pick back through the polished slab gully near 5,000 ft (stemming with the help of trees rooted in the cracks helps on the slicker sections) and down the brushy slope to rejoin the unmaintained Swamp Creek Trail around 3,200 ft. Follow Swamp Creek Trail back down to Swamp Creek Camp on the PCT (re-crossing Swamp Creek on the same log around 3,600 ft), then retrace the Agnes Creek Trail/PCT roughly 8-9 miles to High Bridge and the Stehekin Valley Road for the shuttle or walk back to Stehekin Landing and the ferry. No technical descent gear beyond a single rope/rack for the optional notch rappel is needed; the rest is a sustained, loose, brushy class 2-3 walk-down with real route-finding demands.
Can be firm/icy snow requiring crampons and an ice axe (one May ascent described it as "shockingly icy and smooth" with committing crampon work)

before: Park at the Reflection Lakes pullouts on Stevens Canyon Road (1.4 miles east of the Paradise-Longmire Road junction, roughly 1.9 miles from the Paradise turnoff). The signed Pinnacle Peak Trail (no official trail number; it's a Mount Rainier NP maintained trail) leaves from the south side of the road, directly across from the largest of the Reflection Lakes (approx. 46.7683, -121.7314). The trail climbs moderately through mountain hemlock and Alaska yellow cedar forest for the first half-mile; around 0.5 mi you get a first partial view of Rainier through the trees, and at about 0.6 mi you cross a seasonal stream/cascading creek that is the only reliable water on the hike (dry by late summer in low-snow years). By 0.7 mi the trail breaks out of forest into open talus and heather slopes below the cliffs of Pinnacle Peak, and steepens noticeably from here — this is where lingering snow (well into July on the shaded, north-facing switchbacks) creates the trail's main hazard, since a slip on hard morning snow above the talus can slide a hiker into rock. Around 0.9-1.0 mi the trail passes beneath the impressive cliff bands on Pinnacle's north face, then switchbacks up a short, exposed final pitch (the 'best view on the trail' spot) to reach Pinnacle/Pinnacle Saddle (Pinnacle Gap) at about 1.25-1.3 mi and roughly 5,920-5,960 ft. This saddle is the trail's official end and the crux junction: unmaintained user paths fork east toward Pinnacle Peak/The Castle and west toward Plummer and Denman peaks. For Plummer Peak, continue a short distance past the saddle and look for a climbers' path branching right (west); it crosses a flat rocky shelf holding a seasonal tarn, where a fork continues straight toward Denman — instead bear left (south/uphill) onto the boot path that climbs the open, rocky north-facing slopes of Plummer Peak. This upper section is unmaintained, loose in spots, and route-finding is straightforward but the tread is thin; a short class 2-3 scramble (brief hands-on-rock moves, some loose blocks, mild exposure) gains the last few hundred feet to the 6,374 ft summit. A lingering snowfield often crosses the boot path near the saddle into July — either kick steps straight up it or skirt left on the rockier tread; both options rejoin near the top.

A wiggly crack in mossy rock. Climb through a moss-covered corner ledge, then mossy face climbing to a moss-covered summit jug. Bolts referenced in older published descriptions were not visible on a recent visit ("I think the moss ate them") -- treat as a natural-gear/trad line with a chain anchor at the top.

The standard descent reverses the West Ridge using a sequence of rappels rather than downclimbing the whole route. From the summit area, two single-rope rappels lead down past the crux (5.4-5.6) pitch to a short 3rd-class scramble; this is followed by another single-rope rappel and then a longer double-rope rappel (two ropes joined, or a single 60m doubled) that returns you to the west notch below the technical climbing. Anchors are a mix of fixed slings around horns and flakes; most are solid (slings around big, well-set flakes/horns), but at least one reported station was backed by a sketchy "wad of slings around a handful of small loose rocks" next to the actual load-bearing horn - inspect and back up questionable tat with your own gear. Some parties skip the last downclimb and instead rappel directly down the loose, dirty gully from the notch. Bring a 60m rope (or two ropes for the double-rope stretch) and extra slings/cord to replace weathered anchors. From the notch, descend scree/talus and boot path back into the basin (glissading is possible on lingering snow) to camp, then reverse the approach over Longs Pass to the trailhead. Total rappel count is commonly described as four stations (two singles, a scramble, one more single, then one double-rope rappel); some trip reports collapse this to three rappels depending on how stations are combined, so expect 3-4 total.
The first-ascent account notes protection on 'assorted blocks and horns' in places — inspect placements on the original aid pitches.
It's a long multi-day commitment to even reach the base; weather windows should be confirmed before setting out.

The standard/easiest way up Hard Mox: from a high camp near the Redoubt Glacier/Depot-Redoubt divide, traverse the glacier to the saddle between the Mox Peaks and Mt. Redoubt, descend into the 'Col of the Wild,' gain the Ridge of Gendarmes, then follow ledge/gully systems (West Ledges, Gendarme Notch, East Ledges, Southeast Gullies) to a high notch just left of the summit tower. From the notch, three pitches of loose 4th-to-low-5th-class climbing lead to the top. Per Beckey: most of the climbing is 'more intimidating than technically difficult; if a party finds the climbing above 5.5 they are probably off route.' The route is not sandbagged but is terrifically chossy.

From the summit, take the standard South Arete descent: downclimb the arete (3rd/4th class with a short, more exposed 5th-class section) to the Rabbit Ears, then 3 single-rope rappels (60m rope) from bolted anchors/chains down the gully to the base. Note that the belays on Southern Man itself are described as 'vague and not yet fixed' — this affects the climb, not the descent, but underscores that this route sees less traffic than the East Buttress it starts from, so don't expect a fully bolted rap line down the route itself if you need to bail from the upper headwall; natural anchors would be required there.

before: The crag's namesake and longest route: a 5-pitch, Grade II trad/sport line that 'meanders around following the easiest line' up the tallest formation, with a bolted-plus-small-gear crux roof pitch (5.11c) partway up.
The southwest snowfield below Swiss's summit block hides a running-water spring — a rare reliable water source on an otherwise dry section of the Northern Pickets crest.
From the south (Pickell Pass) side, don't stop at the first high point on the summit ridge — traverse to confirm the true summit, as the ridge has multiple bumps.
Parties approaching from Spectre Plateau to the north report finding 'the easy way up' Swiss from that side, suggesting some route-finding flexibility exists on the peak's north aspect.

First-ascent account (1961): 'ascended to the base of the north ridge, diagonally traversed the northwest face, and reached the summit via the west ridge.' A later trip report (2008) describes the line as a 3rd-class scramble partway up the NE Ridge, then an exposed traverse across the north face on class-4 ledges, followed by an easy class-3 scramble up the remainder of the NW ridge to the top — tricky route-finding on the north-face ledges is the main technical difficulty.
